news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home News Culture – Society With dengue fever cases exceeding 170,000, experts warn that mosquito eradication alone is not enough. (CLO) In the first 10 months of 2026, Vietnam recorded 170,684 cases of dengue fever, with 21 deaths. Given the increasingly unpredictable nature of the epidemic, experts emphasize the need to shift strongly towards proactive prevention, combining mosquito control, vaccination, and epidemiological surveillance. Check Symptoms Công Luận•06/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 On November 6th, the 2026 Dengue Fever Scientific Conference officially commenced, attracting over 700 domestic and international delegates, including representatives from the World Health Organization (WHO), the Ministry of Health, and health sector leaders from 34 provinces and cities. 170,000 cases, the epidemic has spread to mountainous areas. According to figures shared at the conference, dengue fever is currently one of the fastest-growing mosquito-borne infectious diseases in the world , with approximately 100-400 million cases annually. In Vietnam, this disease has created a long-standing healthcare burden for more than four decades. From 1980 to the present, the country has recorded hundreds of thousands of cases each year, and there have been deaths every year. Discover more Buy Bug Kits Book Pest Control Find Treatments Notably, in 2025, Vietnam recorded 184,903 cases. In the first 10 months of 2026, this number continued to be high with 170,684 cases, including 21 deaths. Tìm hiểu lịch sử On November 6th, the Dengue Fever Conference 2026 brought together over 700 domestic and international delegates, along with representatives from the Ministry of Health, WHO, and the health sectors of 34 provinces and cities. Photo: Nguyen Thi Not only has the number of cases increased, but the distribution of the disease has also undergone significant changes. Dengue fever now occurs year-round in provinces and cities, spreading to mountainous areas in the North such as Tuyen Quang and Son La , which previously recorded few cases. Check Symptoms All four serotypes of the Dengue virus (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, DENV-4) are currently circulating in Vietnam. Changes in the dominant serotype over time and across regions, combined with climate change, rapid urbanization, and the emergence of insecticide-resistant mosquitoes, are making disease forecasting and control increasingly complex. You may also like In light of this situation, Dr. Hoang Minh Duc, Director of the Department of Disease Prevention (Ministry of Health), believes that decisive, proactive, and evidence- based disease prevention measures need to be implemented. Referencing and applying international experience adapted to Vietnam's conditions, combined with controlling disease-transmitting mosquitoes and raising public awareness, is crucial in reducing the burden of dengue fever. Check Symptoms Vaccination is incorporated into the overall disease prevention strategy. One of the notable topics at the conference was the practical evidence of the effectiveness of vaccination in preventing dengue fever in several countries. Dr. Rosana Richtmann, Director of the Infection Control Committee at Santa Joana Obstetrics and Gynecology Hospital and former President of the São Paulo Infectious Diseases Society ( Brazil ), stated that Brazil began implementing the dengue fever vaccine in its public immunization program in 2024, initially in 521 localities, and later expanding to 2,752 localities, with 24 million doses distributed. Data from São Paulo in 2024-2025 showed that those who received both doses had a 73.1% reduced risk of symptomatic dengue fever and an 87.9% reduced risk of hospitalization. This protective effect was observed even if the DENV-3 virus type reappeared. Check Symptoms In Indonesia, vaccination is also implemented in conjunction with the application of medical technology to enhance prevention in high-risk areas. Prof. Dr. Nguyen Van Kinh, former Director of the Central Hospital for Tropical Diseases. Photo: Nguyen Thi In Vietnam, one topic of interest is the updates in the draft Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Dengue Fever in 2026, presented by People's Physician, Professor, Doctor Nguyen Van Kinh, former Director of the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases. Check Symptoms You may also like Accordingly, the prevention section emphasizes the role of proactive measures, especially in the context of the current lack of a specific treatment for dengue fever. Recommended solutions include vaccination according to current regulations, monitoring and prevention according to the Ministry of Health's guidelines, and controlling disease-transmitting insects by avoiding mosquito bites and eliminating mosquito larvae. This multi-pronged approach aligns with the WHO's direction for an integrated dengue control strategy, rather than focusing on a single solution. To translate scientific evidence into practice, collaboration between regulatory bodies, healthcare professionals, and partners is identified as crucial. Mr. Benjamin Ping, General Director of Takeda Vietnam, stated that although awareness of dengue fever in Vietnam is relatively high, many people still do not fully understand the risks and severity of the disease for themselves and their families, as well as the necessity of proactive prevention. According to him, it is necessary to strengthen evidence-based preventive measures, with vaccination being an integral part of the overall disease prevention and control strategy. analysis.brief_en: In November 2026, Vietnam reported over 170,000 dengue fever cases, with 21 deaths, highlighting the growing challenge of the disease. The 2026 Dengue Fever Scientific Conference, held on November 6th, brought together over 700 domestic and international delegates, including representatives from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Ministry of Health. Experts warned that mosquito eradication alone is not enough to combat the outbreak, which has spread to mountainous regions like Tuyen Quang and Son La. All four serotypes of the dengue virus (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, DENV-4) are currently circulating in the country. The conference emphasized the need for a multi-pronged approach, combining vaccination, mosquito control, and public awareness. Proactive prevention measures are crucial, as the disease has become more unpredictable due to climate change, urbanization, and insecticide-resistant mosquitoes. The draft guidelines for dengue diagnosis and treatment were also discussed, underscoring the importance of evidence-based strategies in managing the epidemic.

news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế Over 170,000 dengue fever cases, requiring a strong shift towards proactive prevention. In the first 10 months of 2026, Vietnam recorded more than 170,000 cases of dengue fever, a 26% increase compared to the same period last year. Tìm hiểu lịch sử Báo Đầu tư•06/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Given the increasingly complex nature of the epidemic, experts emphasize the need for a change in approach, combining epidemiological surveillance, control of disease-carrying mosquitoes, and vaccination to reduce the risk of illness, hospitalization, and death. Dengue fever is on the rise, posing an increasing challenge to disease control. On November 6th, in Hanoi, the Dengue Fever Conference 2026 brought together over 700 delegates and experts from Vietnam and abroad, along with representatives from the Ministry of Health , the World Health Organization (WHO), and the health sectors of 34 provinces and cities. The conference focused on assessing the epidemiological situation, updating scientific evidence, treatment experiences, and preventive measures against dengue fever, given that the disease continues to place a significant burden on the healthcare system. According to Dr. Hoang Minh Duc, Director of the Department of Disease Prevention (Ministry of Health ), despite Vietnam's implementation of numerous prevention and control measures, dengue fever remains an endemic infectious disease with a high number of cases. Information presented at the conference showed that in the first 10 months of 2026, the whole country recorded 170,684 cases of dengue fever and 21 deaths, an increase of 26% compared to the same period in 2025. The South accounted for 66.8% of the total cases, followed by the Central Highlands at 17.5%, the Central region at 9.8%, and the North at 5.9%. Check Symptoms Previously, in 2025, Vietnam recorded 184,903 cases of dengue fever. These figures continue to reflect the persistent burden of dengue fever, a disease that has been endemic in Vietnam for more than four decades and still records annual deaths. Notably, the epidemiological characteristics are undergoing significant changes. While previously dengue fever typically increased during the rainy season and was concentrated mainly in the South and Central regions, it is now endemic year-round in many localities, including mountainous provinces in the North such as Tuyen Quang and Son La , which previously recorded few cases. With the expansion of its distribution area, all four dengue virus serotypes—DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4—are now present in Vietnam. The dominant serotype changes over time and across regions, with DENV-3 reappearing since late 2024 after many years of infrequent cases. Check Symptoms Surveillance data from the southern region in September 2026 showed that DENV-2 accounted for 69% and DENV-1 for 27.5% of samples with identified viral types. Because post-infection immunity does not provide full protection against other types, people who have had dengue fever are still at risk of reinfection, and may even experience severe symptoms in subsequent infections. Besides the simultaneous circulation of multiple virus types, climate change, erratic weather, rapid urbanization, and the emergence of insecticide-resistant mosquitoes are also making disease forecasting and control more difficult. According to Dr. Hoang Minh Duc, Director of the Department of Disease Prevention (Ministry of Health), despite Vietnam's implementation of numerous prevention and control measures, dengue fever remains an endemic infectious disease with a high number of cases. This reality necessitates continued evaluation of the effectiveness of existing solutions, updating scientific advancements, and selecting more appropriate disease prevention methods. The head of the Department of Disease Prevention emphasized the importance of combining international experience with Vietnam's practical conditions, strengthening control of disease-carrying mosquitoes, and raising public awareness to reduce the burden of disease. Get Health Tips From a treatment perspective, Professor Nguyen Van Kinh, former Director of the Central Hospital for Tropical Diseases, noted that dengue fever can become dangerous even after the patient's fever subsides. The period from the third to the seventh day of the illness is usually the time requiring special monitoring due to the risk of plasma leakage, shock, and serious complications. You may also like Therefore, patients should not be complacent when their fever subsides, but should monitor for warning signs and return for follow-up appointments as instructed. Children, the elderly, and those with underlying health conditions require special attention due to the increased risk of serious complications. Combine vaccination, mosquito control, and epidemiological surveillance. Find Vaccines Given the changing epidemic situation, experts believe that dengue prevention and control strategies need to shift strongly from responding to outbreaks to proactive prevention, with coordinated efforts between management agencies, the health system, and the community. One of the key topics of interest at the Dengue Fever Conference 2026 was the role of vaccination in the overall disease prevention strategy, alongside the mosquito control measures that have been implemented for many years. Dr. Rosana Richtmann, Director of the Infection Control Committee at Santa Joana Obstetrics and Gynecology Hospital and former President of the São Paulo Infectious Diseases Society ( Brazil ), shared her experience in implementing dengue fever vaccination in her country. Brazil began incorporating the vaccine into its public immunization program in 2024, initially in 521 localities, later expanding to 2,752 localities, with approximately 24 million doses distributed. Real-world data from São Paulo in 2024-2025 showed that those who received both doses had a 73.1% reduced risk of symptomatic dengue fever and an 87.9% reduced risk of hospitalization. This protective effect was observed even in the context of the re-emergence of the DENV-3 virus strain. Professor Nguyen Van Kinh presented the updated content in the draft Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Dengue Fever in 2026. These results provide further evidence of the role of vaccination in reducing the burden of dengue fever. However, the protective efficacy depends on the target population, implementation conditions, and epidemiological characteristics, and therefore needs to be considered within the overall framework of disease prevention solutions. In Vietnam, Professor Nguyen Van Kinh presented updated content in the draft Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Dengue Fever in 2026, which was developed based on the 2023 guidelines, incorporating new WHO recommendations and practical treatment experience. The draft focuses on updating the treatment of severe illnesses and complications, integrating guidelines for adults and children; it also adds bedside ultrasound techniques to support the assessment of shock, the risk of recurrent shock, and the selection of appropriate fluid resuscitation options. Notably, the preventive measures in the draft mention combining vaccination according to current regulations with epidemiological surveillance, mosquito bite prevention, larva and pupa eradication, and control of disease-transmitting insects. This approach aligns with the WHO's integrated dengue control guidelines, in which vaccination is one of the preventive tools, not a replacement for mosquito control measures and community involvement. You may also like Experts particularly emphasize the need for proactive disease prevention strategies, given that there is currently no specific antiviral treatment for dengue fever. Effective disease control requires the simultaneous implementation of multiple solutions, from monitoring cases and early detection of outbreaks to organizing timely treatment and raising public awareness of disease prevention. Mr. Benjamin Ping, General Director of Takeda Vietnam, stated that although community awareness of dengue fever is relatively high, many people still do not fully understand the risks and severity of the disease for themselves and their families. Therefore, strengthening evidence-based preventive measures, including appropriate vaccination, should be considered in the overall epidemic prevention and control strategy. At the community level, experts recommend that each family regularly clean their living environment, remove objects that collect water, cover household water containers tightly, eliminate mosquito larvae, and take measures to avoid mosquito bites. Mosquito spraying must follow professional guidelines to ensure effectiveness and safety. Regarding vaccinations, in a previous interview with reporters, doctors from the Long Chau Vaccination System stated that Qdenga is currently the first dengue fever vaccine licensed for circulation in Vietnam. This vaccine contains live attenuated dengue virus, capable of stimulating the body to create an immune response against all four types of dengue virus: DEN-1, DEN-2, DEN-3, and DEN-4. According to research data and practical implementation in many countries, after completing both doses, the vaccine is more than 80% effective in protecting against dengue fever after 12 months and helps reduce the risk of hospitalization by more than 90% after 18 months. Experts consider this a very important step in the fight against dengue fever, especially in the context of the disease becoming increasingly complex and showing an upward trend in many urban areas. analysis.brief_en: Vietnam has reported over 170,000 cases of dengue fever in the first 10 months of 2026, marking a 26% increase compared to the same period in 2025. The Dengue Fever Conference 2026, held on November 6th in Hanoi, highlighted the need for a stronger shift towards proactive prevention strategies. The disease is now endemic year-round in many regions, including previously low-risk mountainous provinces in the North. The conference emphasized the importance of combining vaccination, mosquito control, and epidemiological surveillance to reduce the burden of dengue fever. Updated guidelines for diagnosis and treatment were presented, incorporating new WHO recommendations and practical experience. The dominant serotypes, DENV-2 and DENV-1, were identified in surveillance data, with DENV-3 reappearing after a long absence. Experts stressed that while vaccination can reduce the risk of symptomatic dengue and hospitalization, it must be integrated with other measures, as no specific antiviral treatment exists. The rising cases and changing epidemiological patterns underscore the need for continued evaluation and adaptation of prevention strategies.

supplementary_news.content: On Nov. 5, low-flying helicopters blanketed areas of Florida’s Pinellas and Hillsborough counties with a fine mist. It’s one of the ways Florida health officials hope to slow the country’s largest dengue fever outbreak in more than a decade.Dengue starts with a mosquito bite, so killing the insects is key. The helicopters spray water mixed with Bti , a natural bacteria found in soil that kills black fly and mosquito larvae.Most people become infected when traveling in high dengue risk areas, and Florida had recorded 382 international travel-associated cases as of Oct. 31. But the state has also counted a recent record-high number of people infected on Florida’s turf: 524 .Florida has had domestic dengue outbreaks before. In 2010, it counted 58 locally acquired cases, after nearly eight decades of reprieve . Since then, the largest outbreak was in 2023, when the state reported 189 dengue cases contracted in Florida.As Florida navigates its largest dengue outbreak in more than 15 years, it might help to understand how this virus spreads and how to recognize symptoms and protect yourself. We sought answers to some pressing dengue fever questions.Dengue fever can develop after a person is infected with any of the four dengue viruses . The virus is not transmitted person-to-person , and there is no widely available vaccine to prevent infection.About 3 in 4 people do not get sick, but if symptoms develop, they typically set in about four to 10 days after an infected mosquito’s bite.The most common symptoms of mild dengue fever include high fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, rash, pain behind the eyes, and muscle, joint and bone pain.About 1 in 20 people infected with a dengue virus develops a more severe form of dengue fever, sometimes called dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome. Severe dengue is a life-threatening medical emergency that can cause shock, internal bleeding and death.Warning signs of a severe infection include serious stomach pain or tenderness, vomiting at least three times in 24 hours, bleeding from the gums or nose, rapid breathing, blood in stool or vomit, restlessness, feeling extremely tired and bleeding under the skin that might appear as purplish spots or patches.Those symptoms typically happen 24 to 48 hours after the fever, and they often come on quickly . Anyone experiencing them should seek immediate medical care.There is no specific cure or treatment . Most people recover in about one week, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said . The CDC recommends people rest, hydrate and take acetaminophen to reduce fever and pain. Avoid other pain relievers such as aspirin and ibuprofen because they can raise the risk of bleeding .For severe dengue fever, medical professionals might monitor a patient’s blood pressure and platelet count and provide blood transfusions or intravenous fluid and electrolyte replacement.After being infected with a dengue virus, a person’s immune system learns to fight that type of virus, which helps protect them from reinfection with that same virus. But he or she could remain susceptible to the other three dengue viruses.A person might be asymptomatic or have mild symptoms during an initial dengue infection, and then develop more severe symptoms — or, in rare cases, dengue hemorrhagic fever — after being infected with a second type of dengue virus, said Kristi Miley, a University of Florida public health professor.“Dengue is a doozy, mainly because the second infection can be more dangerous than the first,” Katelyn Jetelina, an epidemiologist and public health expert, said in social media posts .Florida has documented all four dengue viruses since 2009. The type of dengue virus that’s predominantly circulating now “has been noted to cause more severe symptoms than the other three serotypes,” Miley said.Florida’s climate and environment provide ideal conditions for the Aedes species mosquitoes that spread dengue to thrive.If someone travels to a dengue-endemic country and becomes infected even asymptomatically, dengue can enter a community. When a mosquito bites a person infected with the dengue virus, it can introduce the virus to the local mosquito population. An infected female mosquito will remain infected for life — and she can pass the virus to her eggs, which can result in more than 500 infected offspring, said Miley.“When you consider the multiplication equation here and add that to the amount of excessive rainfall that the state has been experiencing this late in the year, one can quickly see how an outbreak of this magnitude can happen,” she said.All told, the previous 16 years saw only 606 total locally acquired cases.“Studies are ongoing to better understand the factors contributing to the dengue activity being seen in Florida in 2026,” said Isabella White, a Florida Department of Health spokesperson.Yes. Not every state has the climate to support Aedes mosquito populations, but any state that does could potentially see local transmission of dengue.In 2025, CDC data showed locally acquired dengue in Florida, California and Arizona.In August, Virginia health officials reported a locally acquired dengue fever infection.The mosquitoes that carry dengue breed in standing water, so health officials urge people to be vigilant about eliminating it around their homes.“Dump or cover any standing water — especially after each time it rains,” Miley said.Florida’s Department of Health recommends discarding old tires and drums, emptying and cleaning birdbaths or pet water bowls at least once or twice a week, and protecting vehicles and boats with tarps so water cannot accumulate.Prevent mosquito bites by using Environmental Protection Agency-registered insect repellents such as DEET and picaridin and covering skin with shoes, socks, and long sleeves and pants.The mosquitoes known to carry dengue are often considered “day biters,” Miley said.If you suspect you’ve been infected with the dengue virus, seek medical attention and avoid exposure to mosquitoes for seven days following symptoms — that’s how long a person would be able to infect mosquitoes, enabling them to spread the disease, Miley said

supplementary_news.content: On Nov. 5, low-flying helicopters blanketed areas of Florida's Pinellas and Hillsborough counties with a fine mist. It's one of the ways Florida health officials hope to slow the country's largest dengue fever outbreak in more than a decade. Dengue starts with a mosquito bite, so killing the insects is key. The helicopters spray water mixed with Bti , a natural bacteria found in soil that kills black fly and mosquito larvae. Most people become infected when traveling in high dengue risk areas, and Florida had recorded 382 international travel-associated cases as of Oct. 31. But the state has also counted a recent record-high number of people infected on Florida's turf: 524 . Florida has had domestic dengue outbreaks before. In 2010, it counted 58 locally acquired cases, after nearly eight decades of reprieve . Since then, the largest outbreak was in 2023, when the state reported 189 dengue cases contracted in Florida. As Florida navigates its largest dengue outbreak in more than 15 years, it might help to understand how this virus spreads and how to recognize symptoms and protect yourself. We sought answers to some pressing dengue fever questions. Dengue fever can develop after a person is infected with any of the four dengue viruses . The virus is not transmitted person-to-person , and there is no widely available vaccine to prevent infection. About 3 in 4 people do not get sick, but if symptoms develop, they typically set in about four to 10 days after an infected mosquito's bite. The most common symptoms of mild dengue fever include high fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, rash, pain behind the eyes, and muscle, joint and bone pain. About 1 in 20 people infected with a dengue virus develops a more severe form of dengue fever, sometimes called dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome. Severe dengue is a life-threatening medical emergency that can cause shock, internal bleeding and death. Warning signs of a severe infection include serious stomach pain or tenderness, vomiting at least three times in 24 hours, bleeding from the gums or nose, rapid breathing, blood in stool or vomit, restlessness, feeling extremely tired and bleeding under the skin that might appear as purplish spots or patches. Those symptoms typically happen 24 to 48 hours after the fever, and they often come on quickly . Anyone experiencing them should seek immediate medical care. There is no specific cure or treatment . Most people recover in about one week, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said . The CDC recommends people rest, hydrate and take acetaminophen to reduce fever and pain. Avoid other pain relievers such as aspirin and ibuprofen because they can raise the risk of bleeding . For severe dengue fever, medical professionals might monitor a patient's blood pressure and platelet count and provide blood transfusions or intravenous fluid and electrolyte replacement. After being infected with a dengue virus, a person's immune system learns to fight that type of virus, which helps protect them from reinfection with that same virus. But he or she could remain susceptible to the other three dengue viruses. A person might be asymptomatic or have mild symptoms during an initial dengue infection, and then develop more severe symptoms — or, in rare cases, dengue hemorrhagic fever — after being infected with a second type of dengue virus, said Kristi Miley, a University of Florida public health professor. "Dengue is a doozy, mainly because the second infection can be more dangerous than the first," Katelyn Jetelina, an epidemiologist and public health expert, said in social media posts . Florida has documented all four dengue viruses since 2009. The type of dengue virus that's predominantly circulating now "has been noted to cause more severe symptoms than the other three serotypes," Miley said. Florida's climate and environment provide ideal conditions for the Aedes species mosquitoes that spread dengue to thrive. If someone travels to a dengue-endemic country and becomes infected even asymptomatically, dengue can enter a community. When a mosquito bites a person infected with the dengue virus, it can introduce the virus to the local mosquito population. An infected female mosquito will remain infected for life — and she can pass the virus to her eggs, which can result in more than 500 infected offspring, said Miley. "When you consider the multiplication equation here and add that to the amount of excessive rainfall that the state has been experiencing this late in the year, one can quickly see how an outbreak of this magnitude can happen," she said. All told, the previous 16 years saw only 606 total locally acquired cases. "Studies are ongoing to better understand the factors contributing to the dengue activity being seen in Florida in 2026," said Isabella White, a Florida Department of Health spokesperson. Yes. Not every state has the climate to support Aedes mosquito populations, but any state that does could potentially see local transmission of dengue. In 2025, CDC data showed locally acquired dengue in Florida, California and Arizona. In August, Virginia health officials reported a locally acquired dengue fever infection. The mosquitoes that carry dengue breed in standing water, so health officials urge people to be vigilant about eliminating it around their homes. "Dump or cover any standing water — especially after each time it rains," Miley said. Florida's Department of Health recommends discarding old tires and drums, emptying and cleaning birdbaths or pet water bowls at least once or twice a week, and protecting vehicles and boats with tarps so water cannot accumulate. Prevent mosquito bites by using Environmental Protection Agency-registered insect repellents such as DEET and picaridin and covering skin with shoes, socks, and long sleeves and pants. The mosquitoes known to carry dengue are often considered "day biters," Miley said. If you suspect you've been infected with the dengue virus, seek medical attention and avoid exposure to mosquitoes for seven days following symptoms — that's how long a person would be able to infect mosquitoes, enabling them to spread the disease, Miley said. supplementary_news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế Proactive measures to prevent and control dengue fever in the face of the risk of widespread outbreaks. The dengue fever epidemic continues to be complex in many localities, with an increase in the number of cases and many outbreaks yet to be brought under control. In response to this situation, the health sector and local authorities are strengthening surveillance, outbreak management, and mosquito control, while also promoting public awareness campaigns. Check Symptoms Báo Tin Tức•09/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Patients with severe dengue fever complications require intervention using advanced, specialized medical equipment. Photo: Dinh Hang/TTXVN The epidemic is developing in a complex manner in many localities. Check Symptoms According to statistics from the Ministry of Health , in the first 10 months of 2026, the whole country recorded 170,684 cases of dengue fever and 21 deaths, while the same period in 2025 recorded approximately 106,000 cases. In 2025, Vietnam had 184,903 cases, the highest in the Asia-Pacific region. The disease is endemic year-round in all provinces and cities, including some mountainous areas in the North that previously recorded few cases, such as Tuyen Quang and Son La. In Ho Chi Minh City, the dengue fever situation continues to worsen. According to the Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control (HCDC), in the week from October 26th to November 1st, the city recorded 1,959 cases, an increase of 16.2% compared to the average of the previous four weeks. From the beginning of the year to the end of today, the city has recorded 44,549 cases and 11 deaths. Discover more Check Symptoms Find Treatments Book Pest Control Doctors at Ho Chi Minh City Children's Hospital have successfully treated a 17-day-old infant with dengue fever and multiple severe complications. The infant, residing in Tan Vinh Loc commune, Ho Chi Minh City, was brought to the hospital in a lethargic state, fussy, with a weak pulse and cold extremities. Prior to admission, the child had a fever for two days – a moderate, intermittent fever – along with startled reactions during sleep and a red rash on the skin. Test results showed a significant decrease in platelets and a positive result for the Dengue virus. Doctors advise parents not to underestimate dengue fever, especially in children. In Dong Nai province , from the beginning of 2026 to the present, the city has recorded 10 deaths due to dengue fever, an increase of 5 cases compared to the same period last year. The entire city has detected 5,651 outbreaks, a 3.6% increase compared to the same period. Localities with high numbers of cases include Nhon Trach, Trang Bom, Binh Phuoc, Minh Hung, Chon Thanh, Tan Trieu, etc. The Dong Nai Center for Disease Control has organized numerous surveillance campaigns in localities with high numbers of cases or recorded deaths; and has also coordinated with the Pasteur Institute and the Institute of Parasitology and Entomology in Ho Chi Minh City to monitor dengue fever prevention and control efforts in many communes and wards throughout the province. Check Symptoms According to a report from the Gia Lai Provincial Department of Health , as of October 27, 2026, the province recorded 9,755 cases of dengue fever, an increase of 6,446 cases and one death compared to the same period in 2025. Of these, the western region accounted for 7,797 cases and one death, representing the majority of the province's total cases. In the week from October 26 to November 1, Gia Lai recorded 612 new cases, concentrated in Phu Tuc, Ia Rsai, Dien Hong, Uar, Pleiku, etc. Cumulatively from the beginning of the year, the province has recorded 474 outbreaks, an increase of 64 outbreaks compared to the same period last year; currently, 76 outbreaks remain uncontrolled. The dengue fever situation in Ho Chi Minh City and other provinces and cities in the southern region remains complex. Therefore, doctors advise people to strictly implement preventive measures recommended by the health sector, such as removing water containers around living areas, maintaining cleanliness in homes and the environment, avoiding mosquito bites by sleeping under mosquito nets, wearing long-sleeved clothing, and using mosquito repellent. Strengthen outbreak control at the grassroots level. You may also like In response to the outbreak, local authorities are implementing various measures to monitor, manage outbreaks, and control disease-carrying mosquitoes. Check Symptoms In Gia Lai , the Chairman of the Provincial People's Committee issued Official Document No. 13307/UBND-KGVX, requesting heads of departments, agencies, and organizations, as well as chairmen of commune and ward People's Committees, to strictly implement dengue fever prevention and control measures as directed by the province and guided by the professional instructions of the Health sector. The goal is to control the disease, reduce the number of cases, and minimize fatalities. The Provincial People's Committee assigned the Department of Health to organize a high-intensity dengue fever prevention and control campaign throughout the province; strengthen surveillance, early detection of cases, and coordinate with local authorities to promptly and thoroughly handle outbreaks. The Health sector is to prepare adequate facilities, equipment, and medicines to ensure the admission, diagnosis, and treatment of patients according to the Ministry of Health's protocol. Medical personnel, local authorities, and residents of Bien Ho commune (Gia Lai province) launched a campaign to clear bushes, clean the environment, and eliminate breeding grounds for mosquitoes that transmit dengue fever. Photo: Quang Thai/TTXVN For localities with a high number of cases, active outbreaks, or potential risks of outbreaks, the Provincial People's Committee requires the establishment of a task force headed by a leader of the commune-level People's Committee, mobilizing local forces to handle the outbreak. Mosquito spraying must be carried out in 100% of households in the outbreak area; and mosquito larva eradication must be organized weekly. Check Symptoms Communes and wards are directly responsible for disease prevention and control in their areas; they direct health stations to act as the focal point for monitoring, early detection of cases, and coordinating the handling of outbreaks. Larva eradication activities must be maintained regularly and periodically, focusing on construction sites, densely populated areas, lodging houses, temporary shelters, and places lacking clean water and with inadequate sanitation. Along with professional measures, the province requires intensified propaganda and mobilization of people to proactively inspect and remove unnecessary water-holding objects, clean the environment, kill mosquitoes, and prevent mosquito bites. The Department of Education and Training coordinates the implementation of disease prevention activities in schools, encouraging students to participate in inspecting water containers and eliminating mosquito larvae at home and at school. In Ho Chi Minh City, the Center for Disease Control and Prevention requested local health centers and health stations to continue closely monitoring the disease situation; and proactively develop plans to organize campaigns to eliminate mosquito larvae and spray chemicals at hotspots. According to the city's Center for Disease Control, the dengue fever outbreak in the area is complex and poses a potential risk of widespread transmission, with cases reported in all 95 communes and wards. The alternating sunny and rainy weather during the peak of the rainy season, along with increased humidity, creates favorable conditions for mosquito breeding, increasing the density of disease vectors and the risk of new outbreaks. To proactively control the outbreak, existing outbreaks need to be thoroughly addressed by combining larval control with mosquito spraying; maintaining the "Weekend Dengue Prevention and Control" campaign; and strengthening public awareness campaigns. Staying up-to-date with scientific advancements promotes proactive prevention. In addition to local disease control measures, the health sector is also paying attention to and discussing the updating of scientific advancements, international experience, and improving the effectiveness of prevention at many domestic and international conferences. You may also like At the Dengue 2026 Conference: “Dengue in Action: Applying Science to Practice Towards Comprehensive Dengue Management,” held over two days from November 5-6, with the participation of more than 700 domestic and international delegates, the Draft Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Dengue Fever in Vietnam in 2026, presented by People's Physician, Professor, Doctor Nguyen Van Kinh, former Director of the Central Tropical Diseases Hospital, included important updates emphasizing the role of dengue prevention, especially since there is currently no specific treatment. Given that dengue fever occurs year-round, experts are calling for the synchronized implementation of proactive prevention measures at all levels, from strengthening epidemiological surveillance and improving treatment capacity to communicating behavioral changes and encouraging appropriate vaccination. Dr. Hoang Minh Duc, Director of the Department of Disease Prevention (Ministry of Health), believes that decisive, proactive, and evidence-based disease prevention measures need to be implemented. Simultaneously, referencing and applying international experiences adapted to Vietnam's context, combined with controlling disease-carrying mosquitoes and raising community awareness, is essential to improve prevention effectiveness and reduce the burden of dengue fever. Given the ongoing dengue outbreak in many localities, along with solutions from the health sector and local authorities, people need to proactively check and remove unnecessary water-holding objects, maintain hygiene in their homes and environments, kill mosquitoes and larvae, and prevent mosquito bites by sleeping under mosquito nets, wearing long-sleeved clothing, and using mosquito repellent. Maintaining regular dengue prevention and control measures, combined with thorough treatment of outbreaks and raising awareness of disease prevention in the community, is crucial to controlling the epidemic, reducing the number of cases, and minimizing fatalities. In the first 10 months of 2026, the country recorded over 170,000 cases of dengue fever, a 26% increase compared to the same period last year, with 21 deaths. Experts warn that the disease can cause shock, multi-organ failure, and even death in adults, including young people without underlying health conditions. Báo Nhân dân•07/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Getting vaccinated against dengue fever. (Photo: VNVC) According to the Department of Disease Prevention ( Ministry of Health ), the South currently accounts for 66.8% of the total dengue fever cases nationwide, followed by the Central Highlands at 17.5%, the Central region at 9.8%, and the North at 5.9%. The disease tends to circulate year-round in many localities, with all four dengue virus types (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, DENV-4) appearing simultaneously. Of these, DENV-1 and DENV-2 are dominant, accounting for approximately 90% of identified samples; DENV-3 was recorded again from the end of 2024 after a period of low detection. Recently, Dong Nai province recorded the deaths of two women, aged 38 and 59, due to dengue shock, one of whom had underlying diabetes. Both self-treated at home and were only hospitalized on the fourth day of their illness in a state of shock, with blood clotting disorders, liver and kidney damage, and damage to multiple organs. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA Previously, the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases admitted a 23-year-old man with no underlying medical conditions who suffered dengue shock and respiratory failure after self-medicating at home for several days. The patient required continuous hemodialysis and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) support for several days before his condition stabilized. Many children are being vaccinated against dengue fever by their parents. According to Dr. Huynh Tran An Khuong, Medical Specialist at VNVC Vaccination System, many adults believe that dengue fever is only dangerous for young children, self-treating at home with over-the-counter medications or delaying medical examinations. In particular, when the fever subsides, patients may mistakenly think they have recovered, when this could be the time when the disease begins to progress dangerously. In fact, the critical phase usually occurs from the 3rd to the 7th day of the illness, when plasma leakage can cause blood concentration, reduced circulating volume, leading to shock, organ damage, and even death if not treated promptly. You may also like Dr. Khuong advises that people with sudden high fever, headache, body aches, or nausea should seek medical attention early. Outpatients with dengue fever must be closely monitored and have follow-up appointments as directed, especially from the 3rd to the 7th day. If severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, restlessness, lethargy, mucosal bleeding, decreased urination, or cold hands and feet occur, they should go to a medical facility immediately, even if the fever has subsided. The elderly , pregnant women, and those with underlying medical conditions should have their risk assessed early. Studies in Malaysia have shown that dengue fever patients hospitalized from the 5th day onwards have a 2.1 times higher risk of acute kidney injury compared to those hospitalized earlier. Notably, a meta-analysis of 21 studies involving nearly 27,000 patients estimated that 1.2% of adults with dengue fever develop acute liver failure; in the group experiencing this complication, the mortality rate reached 47%. A study at the Ho Chi Minh City Hospital for Tropical Diseases estimated the average total cost of an illness to be around US$407, equivalent to VND 10 million according to the study's conversion rate, including treatment costs and lost income. For severe cases requiring intensive care, mechanical ventilation, dialysis, or ECMO, costs can reach hundreds of millions of VND, with some cases reported at VND 120-720 million. After treatment, patients may also experience fatigue, muscle and joint pain, and prolonged reduced concentration, affecting their daily lives and work. According to Doctor An Khuong, in addition to traditional preventive measures such as covering water containers, eliminating mosquito breeding grounds, destroying mosquito larvae, and preventing mosquito bites even during the day, people now have another solution to prevent dengue fever: vaccination. Since September 2024, the VNVC Vaccination System has been administering the Takeda Qdenga dengue fever vaccine, for individuals aged 4 years and older, with a 2-dose regimen administered 3 months apart. The vaccine is designed to generate an immune response against all four dengue virus types (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4), and has been licensed in over 43 countries, with more than 32 million doses distributed as of July 2026. Studies show that the vaccine is more than 80% effective in preventing symptomatic dengue fever caused by any type of dengue virus. At the same time, the vaccine also prevents the risk of severe illness and hospitalization due to dengue fever by more than 90%. Screening for elderly people before vaccination. You may also like Notably, although dengue fever can cause shock, severe bleeding, liver failure, kidney failure, and be life-threatening even in young, healthy individuals, vaccination centers record that adults currently account for less than 30% of the total number of dengue fever vaccine recipients. Dr. Khuong advises adults, especially those with underlying health conditions, who are overweight or obese, or who are elderly, to proactively seek information and advice on getting vaccinated fully, on schedule, and promptly to protect their health. Doctors also note that people who have had dengue fever can still be reinfected because long-term immunity is primarily to the specific virus type they contracted, while cross-immunity to other types is usually only temporary. Some cases of reinfection with a different type carry a higher risk of more severe complications due to antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), although not all reinfections are more serious. Therefore, people who have recovered from dengue fever should still maintain mosquito bite prevention measures and may be advised to get vaccinated after recovery according to professional guidelines. X Culture - Entertainment Culture Entertainment Fashion Nice book Real estate Nice house Zoning Education Education policy Enrollment Marriage and family Family stories Love 360 Rasing child Technology Digital world Wepon - Military Car Car market Driving safe Employment News Labor consulting Labor export 59s Latest News Health Medical - Nutrition - Beautify - Diseases More than 170,000 dengue fever cases, warning of the risk of reinfection Hà Lê - 15:51, Fri Nov 06, 2026 (GMT+7) In the first 10 months of 2026, Vietnam recorded more than 170,000 cases of dengue fever, 21 deaths. People who have been sick are still at risk of re-infection. Dengue fever patients being treated at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases. Photo: BVCC At the Dengue Fever Conference 2026 organized by the Department of Disease Prevention (Ministry of Health) in coordination with relevant units, Dr. Hoang Minh Duc - Director of the Department of Disease Prevention - said that in the first 10 months of 2026, the whole country recorded more than 170,600 cases of dengue fever and 21 deaths. The number of cases increased by 26% compared to the same period in 2025. The South accounted for 66.8% of the total number of cases, the Central Highlands 17.5%, the Central region 9.8% and the North 5.9%. Notably, the disease is tending to circulate year-round, spreading to many localities that previously had fewer cases recorded and no longer followed the clear crop cycle as before. This reality poses an urgent requirement to innovate the epidemic prevention and control strategy in a proactive, comprehensive and scientifically proven direction," Dr. Hoang Minh Duc emphasized. Dr. Hoang Minh Duc - Director of the Department of Disease Prevention (Ministry of Health) - said that although many epidemic prevention and control measures have been implemented, dengue fever is still circulating in Vietnam. Photo: Department of Disease Prevention provided According to Prof. Dr. Nguyen Van Kinh - Chairman of the Vietnam Society of Infectious Diseases, the worrying point is that the diễn biến of the epidemic in recent years is increasingly difficult to predict. After the outbreak in 2022, the number of cases continued to increase, while the disease is no longer clearly concentrated in peak months but may appear year-round. Climate change, changes in rainfall, rapid urbanization and favorable environmental conditions for mosquito breeding are factors contributing to increasing the risk. In particular, all four types of Dengue virus serum (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4) are circulating in Vietnam. The circulation of virus types over time, area, and the situation of mosquito resistance to chemicals make the work of monitoring and forecasting epidemics more complicated. Dr. Hoang Minh Duc emphasized that it is necessary to implement drastic and proactive disease prevention solutions based on scientific evidence; and at the same time apply international experience suitable to Vietnam's conditions, combined with controlling disease-transmitting mosquitoes and raising community awareness. One of the major challenges of dengue fever prevention and control is that the source of infection can exist silently in the community. Many cases of virus infection have no symptoms or atypical manifestations, making it difficult to detect and control the source of infection. In the context that there is currently no specific treatment drug, prevention is identified as a key solution. Experts recommend combining many measures, from epidemiological surveillance, control of mosquitoes and larvae, avoiding mosquito bites to appropriate vaccination and improving diagnostic and treatment capacity. Mr. Benjamin Ping - General Director of Takeda Vietnam - said that although awareness of Dengue hemorrhagic fever is quite high, many people still do not fully understand the risks and severity of the disease. Therefore, it is necessary to promote proactive prevention, implement solutions based on scientific evidence, in which vaccination is part of a comprehensive disease control strategy. Takeda coordinates with partners and health agencies to promote prevention solutions based on scientific evidence, in which vaccination is part of a comprehensive disease control strategy. (Chinhphu.vn) - In the first 10 months of 2026, the whole country recorded 170,684 cases of dengue fever and 21 deaths. Given the increasingly unpredictable nature of the epidemic, experts emphasize the need to implement decisive, proactive, and evidence-based preventive measures. Tìm hiểu lịch sử Báo Chính Phủ•06/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Dengue Fever Conference 2026 - Photo: Nguyen Thi Check Symptoms On November 6th, the 2026 Dengue Fever Scientific Conference officially commenced, attracting over 700 domestic and international delegates, including representatives from the World Health Organization (WHO), the Ministry of Health, and health sector leaders from 34 provinces and cities. With the theme "Dengue in Action: Applying Science to Practice Towards Comprehensive Dengue Management," the conference included 4 thematic sessions, more than 15 in-depth reports, and over 60 scientific research posters, covering the fields of epidemiology, clinical practice, communication, prevention, digital technology, and health policy. The dengue fever situation is becoming increasingly complex: Vietnam needs to shift strongly towards a proactive prevention approach. Discover more Check Symptoms Find Treatments Get Health Tips Dengue fever is one of the fastest-growing infectious diseases transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes worldwide , with approximately 100–400 million cases annually. Check Symptoms In Vietnam, dengue fever has been a persistent burden for over four decades. Since 1980, the country has recorded hundreds of thousands of cases annually, with deaths occurring every year. The incidence rate of dengue fever per 100,000 people is significantly higher than that of other infectious diseases – ranking first in incidence and second in mortality among infectious diseases in Vietnam. In 2025, Vietnam recorded 184,903 cases – the highest in the Asia-Pacific region, surpassing the Philippines , Indonesia, and Bangladesh. In the first 10 months of 2026, the country recorded 170,684 cases and 21 deaths. The disease is endemic year-round in all provinces and cities, spreading to northern mountainous provinces such as Tuyen Quang and Son La – areas that previously recorded few cases. All four serotypes of the Dengue virus (DENV-1, 2, 3, 4) circulate in Vietnam, with the dominant serotype changing over time and region. The rotation of these serotypes, combined with climate change, rapid urbanization, and insecticide-resistant mosquitoes, makes dengue fever increasingly difficult to predict. Dr. Hoang Minh Duc - Director of the Department of Disease Prevention, speaking at the conference - Photo: Nguyen Thi You may also like In light of this situation, Dr. Hoang Minh Duc, Director of the Department of Disease Prevention (Ministry of Health), stated: "We need to implement decisive, proactive, and evidence- based disease prevention measures. Simultaneously, referencing and applying international experiences suitable to Vietnam's context, combined with controlling disease-transmitting mosquitoes and raising community awareness, is essential to improve prevention effectiveness and reduce the burden of dengue fever." Get Health Tips New evidence is shaping the approach to dengue prevention and control. At the plenary session, experts presented evidence showing that vaccination has been implemented and has made concrete progress in many countries. According to Dr. Rosana Richtmann, Director of the Infection Control Committee (ICC) at Santa Joana Obstetrics and Gynecology Hospital and former President of the Infectious Diseases Society of São Paulo, Brazil, the country has implemented the dengue fever vaccine in its public immunization program since 2024, starting in 521 localities and expanding to all 2,752 localities, with 24 million doses distributed. Actual data from São Paulo in 2024–2025 shows that receiving two doses reduces the risk of symptomatic dengue fever by 73.1% and the risk of hospitalization by 87.9%. The protective effect is maintained even if the DENV-3 strain reappears. In Indonesia , the vaccine is also being deployed in conjunction with the application of medical technology in proactive prevention in high-risk areas. Dr. Rosana Richtmann - Director of the Infection Control Committee (ICC), Santa Joana Obstetrics and Gynecology Hospital, former President of the São Paulo Infectious Diseases Society, Brazil, shared her insights at the conference. - Photo: Nguyen Thi According to People's Physician, Professor, Doctor Nguyen Van Kinh, former Director of the Central Tropical Diseases Hospital, more than 90% of people infected with the Dengue virus show no clinical symptoms but can still become a source of transmission. In addition, climate change, urbanization, and the development of insecticide-resistant mosquitoes are making the disease more difficult to predict and control. He also noted that the disease typically progresses through a fever phase and a critical phase. Between the 3rd and 7th day of the illness, even when the fever subsides, complications can still occur. Therefore, patients should not be complacent when their fever goes down but should continue to monitor for warning signs and return for follow-up appointments as directed by their doctor. Currently, there is no specific treatment for dengue fever. Professor Nguyen Van Kinh believes that a combination of vaccination, mosquito and larva eradication, and timely treatment is necessary to reduce the number of cases and limit fatalities. Vaccination is one of the preventive measures that needs attention, combined with eliminating stagnant water sources, limiting mosquito breeding grounds, and strengthening communication to encourage people to proactively prevent the disease. People's Teacher, Professor, Doctor Nguyen Van Kinh speaking at the Conference - Photo: Nguyen Thi Combining multiple proactive preventive measures simultaneously is seen as a policy signal consistent with WHO recommendations on an integrated dengue control strategy. You may also like For scientific advancements to be progressively applied in practice, coordination between regulatory agencies, professionals, and healthcare partners plays a crucial role. For the second consecutive year as a scientific partner of the Dengue Summit, Takeda Pharmaceutical Vietnam Co., Ltd. supports efforts to promote evidence-based prevention solutions, contributing to raising public awareness about dengue fever. Benjamin Ping, General Director of Takeda Vietnam, shared: "Although awareness of dengue fever in Vietnam is relatively high, research shows that the majority of people still do not fully understand the risks and severity of the disease for themselves and their families, as well as the urgency of proactive prevention. Therefore, it is necessary to strengthen proactive prevention measures to reduce the burden of dengue fever in Vietnam. Takeda is collaborating with international partners and health agencies to support evidence-based prevention solutions aimed at protecting public health, with vaccination being part of the overall disease prevention and control strategy." Given that dengue fever occurs year-round, experts are calling for the synchronized implementation of proactive preventive measures at all levels – from strengthening epidemiological surveillance and improving treatment capacity to communicating behavioral changes and encouraging appropriate vaccination. The dengue fever vaccine currently available in Vietnam is the first and only one approved by the Ministry of Health. It is also recommended by the WHO for use in countries with a high dengue burden and has achieved WHO pre-qualification for quality, safety, and efficacy. To date, the vaccine has been approved in 43 countries, with over 32 million doses distributed globally, and is being implemented in public immunization programs in Brazil, Argentina, Colombia, Indonesia, Honduras, Paraguay, Peru, and Thailand. supplementary_news.content: News Sports Entertainment Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals STATE Florida dengue outbreak reaches 524 cases, here's where, how to avoid Cheryl McCloud C. A. Bridges USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Updated Nov. 6, 2026, 12:08 p.m. ET The historic surge in dengue fever continues. Florida reported 39 more locally acquired cases in one week, according to the latest update from the Florida Department of Health. The disease is also called breakbone fever, due to the pain it causes. That brings the statewide total for the year to 524 as of Oct. 31, the largest outbreak in the United States in decades. The previous record for Florida cases in recent memory was 199 in 2023. In 2025, Florida reported 62 cases. The numbers may climb even higher in the weeks ahead after record rainfall left roads flooded, ditches full, and standing water in many Florida yards. ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection The bulk of the cases continues to be in Hillsborough County on Florida's west coast, which has 407 confirmed cases. Locally acquired cases have now been reported in 12 counties. The outbreak prompted Hillsborough County Administrator Bonnie Wise to issue a state of local emergency, which expires Nov. 12 unless the county extends it again as officials "work to control the mosquito population and protect residents from dengue fever." One death has been confirmed in Hillsborough County, identified as 80-year-old Gay Small, who died of “dengue infection” along with septic shock and multi-organ failure, according to a death certificate. Florida's outbreak far exceeds the previous largest outbreak, which was 264 local cases in Hawaii's Big Island between September 2015 and March 2016. President Trump in September issued an order for a "campaign" to reduce the mosquito and tick population in Washington, D.C. That model could then be "applied as targeted, innovative, non-chemical pest control for the whole nation." Dengue isn't the only mosquito-transmitted disease that has been this year in Florida, although those have been in far fewer numbers than dengue: West Nile Virus, Chikungunya and Eastern Equine Encephalitis. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites, including advice from the Florida Department of Health. 20 counties under mosquito-borne illness advisories, alerts A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Bay Brevard Broward Holmes Leon Manatee Martin Palm Beach Polk Sarasota Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Citrus Duval Hillsborough Miami-Dade Orange Pasco Pinellas Seminole "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease-capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." Dengue cases continue to climb in Florida According to Florida Department of Health data released Nov. 6, 12 counties have reported 524 locally acquired dengue cases, up from 485 reported Oct. 24. There have also been eight positive samples of locally acquired West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. Dengue: 524 cases 407 in Hillsborough County 80 in Pinellas County 12 in Miami-Dade County 10 in Orange County 4 in Pasco County 3 in Citrus County 2 in Manatee County 1 in Brevard County 1 in Broward County 1 in Palm Beach County 1 in Polk County West Nile: eight cases 2 in Alachua County 2 in Duval County ( incuding one asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Holmes County 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Sarasota County 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 1 case 1 in Miami-Dade County Eastern Equine Encephalitis: 1 case 1 in Leon County What is Hillsborough County doing to try to control mosquitoes? A local state of emergency in Hillsborough County expires Nov. 12. A state of local emergency can be in effect for only seven days, unless rescinded or extended, according to the Hillsborough County Department of Health. "Mosquito management crews are increasing treatments by air and ground because the county’s mosquito surveillance in many neighborhoods is showing dengue virus activity in the mosquito population. "Residents are encouraged to look for and eliminate standing water on their property after recent heavy rains." Residents can sign up to be notified where aerial treatment will occur in neighborhoods. You can also go to the county's website to see when and where mosquito "operations" are scheduled to take place. Trump wants mosquitoes, ticks eliminated in Washington, D.C. On Sept. 29, Trump signed an executive order to eliminate ticks and mosquitoes in Washington, D.C. The order directs the Secretary of the Interior, the Secretary of Agriculture, the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Administrator of General Services, along with the Secretary of Health and Human Services, to "develop and implement a campaign across Washington, D.C., to reduce invasive mosquito populations by 90 percent and the tick population by 50 percent by 2028 using safe and effective, non-chemical, and innovative technology-enabled methods. "This new model, localized to Washington, D.C., can later be applied nationwide as targeted, innovative, non-chemical pest control for the whole nation." Florida residents should take precautions to avoid mosquito-borne illnesses "Residents throughout the state should continue to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying bug spray, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible — especially during sunrise and sunset when mosquitos are most active," said Isabella White, FDOH press secretary via email Sept. 23. White said FDOH "continues to coordinate with local mosquito control partners to support surveillance and targeted response efforts in affected areas. These efforts help reduce mosquito populations, limit the risk of disease transmission, and protect residents across Florida." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Why is dengue called 'breakbone fever?' Dengue is sometimes called “breakbone fever” because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine. Is dengue contagious? Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight, or premature birth. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. The retrospective observational study evaluated laboratory-confirmed cases to map the precise geographic and temporal dimensions of infection, providing critical spatial resolution for public health agencies aiming to deploy reactive vector control measures. By analyzing geographic coordinates linked to patient residences alongside official consultation dates, the investigative team demonstrated that local transmission events routinely concentrate within tightly defined neighborhood boundaries while persisting across shifting climatic periods. Dengue remains an endemic public health concern throughout Valle del Cauca, yet the exact spatial scale and temporal timing of seasonal transmission necessary to execute effective reactive interventions have historically remained unclear across the department’s forty-two municipalities. To resolve this operational gap, the authors established two primary research aims. The first focused on identifying statistically significant spatio-temporal dengue clusters within defined municipal zones. The secondary aim evaluated the relationship between patients’ demographic and clinical characteristics and their likelihood of requiring hospitalization for dengue care. The investigation drew data directly from the Sistema Nacional de Vigilancia en Salud Pública, Colombia’s national public health surveillance network known as SIVIGILA. Healthcare providers across Valle del Cauca reported a total of 3,964 dengue cases during the 2022 calendar year, of which 2,232 cases—or 56 percent—were confirmed through laboratory diagnostics. For the purpose of spatial analysis, the investigators utilized each patient’s documented residential geolocation as the probable site of viral infection. Among the laboratory-confirmed records, 1,973 cases fell within the specified spatial boundaries of nine municipalities selected for detailed clustering assessment, which was executed using Kulldorff’s space-time scan statistic and mapped using the R programming environment. Discover more Engineering job board Research publication platform Scientific instrument sales Laboratory equipment supplier The space-time scan statistic uncovered twenty-eight distinct clusters at the sub-municipal level, encompassing radii between 0 and 0.98 kilometers. These transmission foci endured for durations spanning one to six months and contained case counts ranging from 10 to 114 individuals. In total, the identified clusters accounted for 32.0 percent of the 1,973 cases analyzed within the nine municipalities. Notably, twenty-six of the twenty-eight clusters—representing 92.9 percent—spanned both warm-dry and cool-wet seasonal phases, demonstrating that localized viral activity regularly bridged contrasting meteorological periods rather than confining itself exclusively to a single seasonal window. Beyond mapping spatial boundaries, the research team analyzed factors driving severe disease manifestations, noting that 960 patients within the overall cohort were hospitalized. Multivariable evaluations revealed substantial disparities across socioeconomic brackets and age groups. Patients classified within a lower socioeconomic status faced an estimated 30 percent increase in the odds of hospitalization compared to individuals of higher economic standing, with an odds ratio of 1.30 and a 95 percent confidence interval between 1.07 and 1.57. Furthermore, individuals enrolled in Colombia’s state-subsidized health insurance scheme exhibited significantly elevated odds of hospital admission compared to those participating in the contributory insurance system, reflected by an odds ratio of 1.74 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.41 to 2.15. Age also represented a key determinant of clinical escalation, as individuals aged 70 years or older experienced more than double the odds of hospital admission compared to younger adults between the ages of 20 and 29 years, yielding an odds ratio of 2.47 and a 95 percent confidence interval from 1.51 to 4.04. The authors concluded that pinpointing sub-municipal dengue clusters reveals highly actionable spatial targets capable of guiding reactive local mosquito control programs, while underscoring that dengue places an unequal burden on socioeconomically vulnerable communities and older populations in Valle del Cauca. The Tampa Bay area remains the epicenter of a nationwide Dengue Fever outbreak. Hundreds of cases have been reported in Hillsborough and Pinellas counties, but will an upcoming cold front help stop the spread? FOX 13's Blake DeVine reports. The Brief Cooler temperatures could temporarily slow mosquitoes spreading dengue across the Tampa Bay area, although experts say a freeze is needed to significantly reduce their population. Florida has recorded 524 locally acquired dengue cases this year, with Hillsborough County accounting for most infections. Hillsborough County has extended its local emergency through Nov. 12 as mosquito control crews continue aerial and ground treatments. TAMPA, Fla. - An incoming cold front could temporarily suppress the aggressive insects driving Florida's historic dengue fever outbreak, though health experts warn only freezing temperatures can stop transmission. Cold weather brings brief relief The backstory: The virus primarily spreads through infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which thrive in Florida's warm climate. Dr. Nicole Iovine, UF Health's chief epidemiologist, says the approaching cold front could help reduce mosquito activity without eliminating the insects. "The lower temperature helps because the mosquitoes will be less active," she said. "So, 50 degrees, that's good. But as far as actually killing off the population, you need at least one night of a good freeze." Travel sparks local transmission Dig deeper: Iovine says the outbreak is particularly unusual because locally acquired dengue cases have historically been concentrated in South Florida. She believes infected travelers may have introduced the virus to mosquitoes in the Tampa Bay area, allowing it to spread locally. Florida dengue numbers surge By the numbers: Florida has confirmed 524 locally acquired dengue cases this year, alongside more than 900 total illnesses when counting travel-related infections, according to the Florida Department of Health. Local case tallies include: Hillsborough County: 407 cases Pinellas County: 80 cases Pasco County: 4 cases Hillsborough steps up treatments What's next: Hillsborough County leads Florida in locally acquired infections and has extended its state of local emergency through Thursday, Nov. 12. Mosquito control crews are increasing aerial and ground treatments across the county, targeting both adult mosquitoes and larvae. Hillsborough County Mosquito Management senior environmental scientist Paolo Pecora says the county is working to interrupt the mosquito life cycle. "We want to knock down the adult mosquitoes that are actively spreading the virus," Pecora said. Pecora says targeted treatments have reduced Aedes aegypti mosquito populations by 97% in the East Lake area. Dengue symptoms Why you should care: Dengue symptoms can include severe headaches, body aches, fever, nausea, vomiting and a rash. Some infected people experience mild symptoms or none at all. Iovine says people experiencing these symptoms should contact a health care provider about testing, particularly if they have no respiratory symptoms. There is no specific antiviral medication to treat dengue. Doctors typically recommend rest, plenty of fluids and acetaminophen, commonly known as Tylenol, to help manage mild symptoms. Patients should avoid ibuprofen and aspirin because they can increase the risk of bleeding. Unusual bleeding, severe abdominal pain or persistent vomiting require immediate medical attention. Protecting homes from mosquitoes What you can do: Homeowners can protect their properties by dumping standing water from flowerpots, buckets, tires and outdoor bins. Anyone heading outdoors should wear long protective sleeves and apply bug repellent formulated with DEET or picaridin. Residents can check upcoming neighborhood spray routes on the Hillsborough County Mosquito Operations website. The Source: Information for this story came from data from the Florida Department of Health, statements from Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services, interviews with UF Health's chief epidemiologist and previous reporting on FOX 13.
