supplementary_news.content: Dengue fever is unpredictable, with 21 deaths recorded so far. In Vietnam, dengue fever has been a persistent burden for over four decades. Since 1980, the country has recorded hundreds of thousands of cases annually, with deaths occurring every year. Find Treatments VietnamPlus • 06/11/2026 In the first 10 months of this year, the whole country recorded more than 170,600 cases of dengue fever and 21 deaths. The number of cases increased by 26% compared to the same period in 2025. The South accounted for 66.8% of the total cases, the Central Highlands 17.5%, the Central region 9.8%, and the North 5.9%. Mr. Hoang Minh Duc, Director of the Department of Disease Prevention ( Ministry of Health ), stated this at the Dengue Fever Conference 2026, which was attended by over 700 domestic and international delegates and was organized by the Department of Disease Prevention (Ministry of Health ) on November 6th in Hanoi. According to Mr. Hoang Minh Duc, despite the implementation of numerous disease prevention and control measures, dengue fever is still prevalent in Vietnam. Given the increasingly unpredictable nature of the disease, the health sector is reviewing and evaluating the effectiveness of existing solutions, updating scientific advancements, and seeking more proactive and appropriate preventive measures. Discover more Check Symptoms Find Grief Support Get Health Tips In Vietnam, dengue fever has been a persistent burden for over four decades. Since 1980, the country has recorded hundreds of thousands of cases annually, with deaths occurring every year. The incidence rate of dengue fever per 100,000 people is significantly higher than other infectious diseases – ranking first in incidence and second in mortality among infectious diseases in Vietnam. Find Treatments In 2025, Vietnam recorded 184,903 cases – the highest in the Asia-Pacific region, surpassing the Philippines , Indonesia, and Bangladesh. In the first 10 months of 2026, the country recorded 170,684 cases. The disease is endemic year-round in all provinces and cities, spreading to even the northern mountainous provinces such as Tuyen Quang and Son La – areas that previously recorded few cases. All four serotypes of the Dengue virus (DENV-1, 2, 3, 4) circulate in Vietnam, with the dominant serotype changing over time and across regions. The rotation of these serotypes, combined with climate change, rapid urbanization, and insecticide-resistant mosquitoes, makes dengue fever increasingly difficult to predict. You may also like 170,000 dengue fever cases in 10 months: Is the epidemic changing its pattern? According to statistics, from the beginning of 2026 to the present, the whole country has recorded more than 170,000 cases of dengue fever and 21 deaths. Dengue fever no longer follows a cyclical pattern; a strong shift towards proactive prevention is necessary. In the first 10 months of 2026, the whole country recorded more than 170,000 cases of dengue fever and 21 deaths. Over 170,000 dengue fever cases, requiring a strong shift towards proactive prevention. In the first 10 months of 2026, Vietnam recorded more than 170,000 cases of dengue fever, a 26% increase compared to the same period last year. In light of this situation, the Director of the Department of Disease Prevention stated that it is necessary to implement decisive, proactive, and evidence- based disease prevention measures. Simultaneously, referencing and applying international experiences adapted to Vietnam's context, combined with controlling disease-carrying mosquitoes and raising public awareness, is essential to improve prevention effectiveness and reduce the burden caused by dengue fever. Find Treatments Professor Nguyen Van Kinh - Former Director of the Central Hospital for Tropical Diseases. (Photo: PV/Vietnam+) Professor Nguyen Van Kinh, former Director of the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, stated that after the 2022 outbreak, the number of dengue fever cases continued to increase. Notably, the disease no longer follows a clear seasonal or cyclical pattern as before. Currently, all four types of Dengue virus (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4) are circulating in Vietnam. Types 1 and 2 are dominant, accounting for approximately 90% of cases. Significantly, type 3 reappeared from the end of 2024, after many years of not being detected. Surveillance data from the southern region in September 2026 showed that DENV-2 accounted for 69% and DENV-1 accounted for 27.5% of the samples in which the virus type was identified. Because there is no cross-immunity between the virus types, a person can contract dengue fever up to four times. Find Treatments The scene at the conference. (Photo: PV/Vietnam+) Notably, the Draft Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Dengue Fever in Vietnam 2026, presented by Professor Nguyen Van Kinh at the conference, includes important updates in the prevention chapter: emphasizing the crucial role of dengue prevention, especially since there is currently no specific treatment. The draft guidelines recommend combining measures such as dengue vaccination according to current regulations with surveillance and prevention as prescribed by the Ministry of Health , and control of disease-transmitting insects (avoiding mosquito bites, eliminating larvae and pupae). Find Treatments You may also like Combining proactive preventive measures simultaneously is seen as a policy signal consistent with WHO recommendations on an integrated dengue control strategy. With the theme “Dengue in Action: Applying Science to Practice Towards Comprehensive Dengue Management,” the conference included four thematic sessions and more than 15 in-depth reports covering the fields of epidemiology, clinical practice, communication, prevention, digital technology , and health policy. (James Gathany/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention via AP, File) NEW YORK — Florida’s current dengue outbreak is the largest in several decades of any U.S. state. State health officials reported this week that nearly 300 locally acquired cases of the mosquito-borne disease have been tallied so far this year. The vast majority of them were in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa. Federal health officials say their data on dengue outbreaks is limited. But available information from state health departments and medical journals suggests the Florida outbreak marks the most cases in a calendar year for any state since at least the 1940s. Puerto Rico is consistently hit hard by dengue, with numbers much higher than what’s seen in any of the 50 states. But in the continental U.S., Florida usually gets the most locally transmitted cases. The state’s previous worst year was 2023, when just under 200 locally spread cases were reported. Officials in Hillsborough and surrounding counties have declared local emergencies, and workers in the Tampa area are spraying day and night to tamp down the population of disease-transmitting mosquitoes. What is dengue? Dengue (pronounced DEHN’-gay) is caused by a virus spread by a type of mosquito. Many infected people don’t get sick, but some experience fever, flu-like symptoms and — notoriously — aches. It’s been nicknamed “breakbone fever” for the excruciating pain some people experience. Severe cases can cause bleeding, shock and death. There has been one dengue death in Florida this year — an elderly Tampa woman on Sept. 4. Other Tampa-area cases that have gone to the hospital were patients treated for fever and dehydration, said Carla Fry, Hillsborough County’s health officer. There are four types of dengue virus, simply known as 1, 2, 3 and 4. When someone is first infected, their body builds antibodies against that type for life. If they get infected with another type of dengue, the antibodies from the first infection may fail to neutralize the second type — and actually can help the virus enter immune cells and replicate. That’s made it difficult to develop an effective vaccine. Most people in the Tampa area don’t have prior immunity to any form of dengue, said Dawn Wesson, a Tulane University expert on dengue and other diseases spread by mosquitoes. How does dengue spread? The warm-weather mosquitoes that spread dengue live in Florida and some other hotter U.S. locales, but experts say they have been expanding their geographic reach because of climate change. For decades, most continental U.S. infections were found among people who caught the virus while traveling internationally, along with locally acquired cases in Puerto Rico. But in 2009-2010, Key West, Florida, reported the first dengue cases acquired in the continental U.S. outside of the Texas-Mexico border since 1945. The largest outbreak of dengue in any U.S. state since then occurred in Hawaii, where 264 locally acquired cases were reported over a six-month span in 2015-2016. The Tampa-area outbreak, which first came to light in July, has now surpassed that. Across the world, more than 2.2 million infections and nearly 1,200 deaths have been reported this year, according to the World Health Organization. There have been more than 1,600 locally acquired U.S. cases this year, most of them in Puerto Rico, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Why is it so bad in Tampa? Florida tends to get a lot of dengue in part because the state receives a lot of travellers who have been to Puerto Rico or other places where the disease is present, Wesson said. Usually most cases are in southern Florida, around the Miami area. It’s hard to say what’s happening in the Tampa area this year, but the surge may be at least partly related to travel patterns, she added. Locally acquired cases in Florida have actually surpassed travel-associated cases, by a count of 252 to 245 as of last week. But it’s close, and at least 13 Hillsborough County cases were diagnosed in travelers, according to the state. Traditionally, the CDC would be highly visible in a situation like this, but it hasn’t been this time, Wesson noted. The U.S. public health agency has to be invited in by state officials, and Florida officials have not asked for CDC disease investigators to come in, CDC spokesman Jason McDonald said. The agency has provided $800,000 in assistance to the state health department, although Tampa-area officials this week said they haven’t seen that aid trickle down to the local level yet. The Florida Department of Health said it plans to use the CDC money for community outreach, lab testing and pesticide control. What can you do to prevent infection? The current outbreak is centered just north of Tampa, and workers have been spraying to kill mosquitoes. They also have been checking properties for pooled water, including in tires, where mosquitoes might breed. People in an outbreak area can take their own steps for protection, experts say. The virus-carrying mosquitoes can bite any time of day, so it’s important for people in an outbreak area to apply EPA-registered insect repellents containing active ingredients like DEET, experts say. Wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and long pants to cover the skin and make it harder for mosquitoes to bite. Staying indoors, behind screens or in rooms with air conditioning will also lessen the chances for a bite. Those steps are especially important just after sunrise and around sunset, when mosquitoes tend to be most active, researchers say. People should also check their property and get rid of any pooled water where mosquitoes might breed. Climate conditions and persistent mosquito populations will likely make local dengue outbreaks a more frequent problem, Wesson said. “There’s a good chance that this is the new normal,” she said. ___ The Associated Press’ health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism and private foundations. With over 42,500 cases and 11 deaths due to dengue fever in Ho Chi Minh City from the beginning of the year to the end of week 43/2026, this familiar disease still poses many potential risks. Báo Đầu tư•08/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Dengue fever is not unfamiliar to the Vietnamese people, but the continuous recording of severe cases and deaths shows that the danger of this infectious disease is still not fully understood. Check Symptoms By the end of week 43/2026, Ho Chi Minh City recorded over 42,500 cases of dengue fever, including 11 deaths. Di An ward alone accounted for 861 cases and one child death. These figures reflect the burden of the epidemic and highlight the urgent need for early detection, timely treatment, and improved prevention effectiveness. Nationwide, in the first 10 months of 2026, the country recorded 170,684 cases of dengue fever and 21 deaths, a 26% increase compared to the same period in 2025. The South accounted for 66.8% of the total cases, followed by the Central Highlands at 17.5%, the Central region at 9.8%, and the North at 5.9%. Patients with dengue fever are being treated at a medical facility. Previously, in 2025, Vietnam recorded 184,903 cases of dengue fever. These figures continue to reflect the persistent burden of dengue fever, a disease that has been endemic in Vietnam for more than four decades and still records annual deaths. Tìm hiểu lịch sử Notably, the epidemiological characteristics are undergoing significant changes. While previously dengue fever typically increased during the rainy season and was concentrated mainly in the South and Central regions, it is now endemic year-round in many localities, including mountainous provinces in the North such as Tuyen Quang and Son La , which previously recorded few cases. Discover more Check Symptoms Find Treatments Read Travel Guides According to Dr. Dinh Van Thoi, Deputy Head of the Multidisciplinary Clinic at the Pasteur Institute of Ho Chi Minh City, Dengue fever is an acute infectious disease caused by the Dengue virus, with four serotypes: DEN-1, DEN-2, DEN-3, and DEN-4. The disease is primarily transmitted through the bite of the Aedes aegypti mosquito carrying the virus, can affect people of all ages, and can erupt into epidemics. Read Travel Guides Despite years of disease prevention campaigns, the number of cases remains alarmingly high due to the combined impact of several factors. These include climate change and variations in temperature and rainfall, which can disrupt the breeding seasons and distribution of disease-carrying mosquitoes, prolonging outbreaks in some areas. Urbanization, high population density, and inadequate sanitation also create favorable conditions for mosquito breeding, increasing the risk of transmission. Small objects that hold stagnant water in homes, gardens, or residential areas can become breeding grounds for mosquito larvae if not regularly inspected and treated. In addition, travel, tourism , and trade contribute to an increased risk of virus spread between localities. People carrying the Dengue virus can travel to other areas, creating conditions for local mosquitoes to receive the virus and continue to transmit the disease. The worrying aspect is that dengue fever can progress from mild to severe in a short period of time. Many cases initially present with only fever, headache, and body aches, easily mistaken for common viral infections. However, the disease can develop into plasma leakage, severe bleeding, shock, and organ damage. You may also like Dr. Thoi noted that young children, especially those under one year old, may exhibit atypical symptoms such as fever, poor feeding, loss of appetite, or abdominal pain, making it difficult to identify the disease. Pregnant women with dengue fever are at risk of complications affecting both mother and fetus, and vaginal bleeding requires urgent examination to differentiate it from other obstetric conditions. Find Treatments For the elderly or those with underlying conditions such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, chronic liver disease, or kidney disease, dengue fever can complicate their health, increase the risk of complications, and prolong treatment time. In particular, patients need to be closely monitored during the period from the third to the seventh day after the onset of fever, as warning signs often appear at this time, even when body temperature begins to decrease. Symptoms such as severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, restlessness, cold extremities, or decreased urination require immediate medical evaluation. With dengue fever continuing to put pressure on the healthcare system, the availability of a vaccine in Vietnam is seen as a significant step forward, adding another tool to protect public health. Ms. Do Cao Van Anh, a senior advisor at Long Chau Pharmacy and Vaccination System, stated that the Dengue virus has four serotypes, meaning that individuals who have previously had dengue fever can be reinfected with a different serotype. Some subsequent infections may have a higher risk of severe complications due to antibody-dependent enhancement mechanisms. The availability of the Qdenga vaccine opens up more opportunities for proactive disease prevention, helping to reduce the risk of dengue fever and some of its serious consequences. However, the vaccine has only recently been introduced and is not yet part of the Expanded Immunization Program, while its reach and coverage in the community remain limited. Find Vaccines According to Doctor Van Anh, the Qdenga vaccine is licensed in Vietnam for people aged 4 and older, with a two-dose schedule three months apart. Individuals who have or have not had dengue fever can be assessed for vaccination; prior testing for dengue infection is not mandatory. Notably, vaccination should be administered according to professional guidelines, especially for individuals with underlying medical conditions or special health circumstances. The vaccine is contraindicated for pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, individuals with significant immunosuppression, and those with a history of severe hypersensitivity reactions to vaccine components or previous doses. Individuals with acute illnesses and high fevers should postpone vaccination until their health stabilizes. For those who have recently recovered from dengue fever, the timing of vaccination should be advised by a doctor; some guidelines recommend waiting about six months after recovery. Women planning to become pregnant should complete vaccination at least one month before their expected pregnancy. According to Dr. Luu Hong Ngoc Phuong of Gia Dinh People's Hospital, people currently suffering from dengue fever should prioritize treatment and monitoring for warning signs, and should not receive vaccinations during the acute phase of the disease. Vaccination after recovery must be evaluated through a screening examination to ensure safety. You may also like However, experts agree that vaccines cannot replace measures to prevent mosquito bites and eliminate mosquito breeding grounds. Dengue fever is not transmitted directly through shaking hands, talking, or hugging, but mainly through Aedes mosquitoes carrying the virus. Therefore, controlling the disease vector remains crucial in epidemic prevention. The health sector recommends that each family spend at least 10 minutes each week checking for and removing stagnant water sources and mosquito larvae inside and outside the house. Easily overlooked locations such as flower vases, water bowls on altars, plant pot saucers, water containers, or discarded bottles and cans can all become breeding grounds for mosquitoes. In fact, even a very small amount of water remaining in a can lid or forgotten item can create ideal conditions for mosquitoes to lay eggs. Therefore, covering water containers, collecting waste, turning unused items upside down, and proactively preventing mosquito bites should become regular habits. Beyond individual families, schools and communities also play a crucial role in maintaining disease prevention activities. Schools need to guide students in identifying mosquito breeding grounds and practicing environmental hygiene at home. Local authorities, organizations, and community health forces need to coordinate efforts to encourage people to collect waste, dispose of items that collect standing water, and monitor the risk of disease-carrying mosquitoes. After decades of facing dengue fever, advances in medicine have brought about additional preventative solutions through vaccination. However, effective community protection still depends on a combination of appropriate vaccination, early detection, timely treatment, and environmental control. supplementary_news.content: Ask AIReal-time News Market Earnings CallEvent Calendar More Earnings CallEvent CalendarWatchlistPodcastMarket InfluencersMore Ask AIReal-time News WatchlistHoldingsMarketEarnings CallEvent CalendarPodcastMarket Influencers Dengue Challenge Study Finds Less Virus, Better Immunity — and a Shortcut for Vaccine Testing 2026-11-08 06:08 (GMT+0) Add preferred source In a 45-person dengue human challenge study, the highest viremia produced the weakest, fastest-fading immune responses, while moderate replication produced the most durable immunity — a direct challenge to the idea that bigger, faster immune activation is better. Serum enhancement of dengue-3 infection at a 1:10 dilution was the single strongest predictor of high viremia, and only people with multiple prior infections carried the broadly neutralizing EDE antibodies linked to near-sterilizing protection. The findings give dengue vaccine developers a cheap cell-culture assay for enhancement risk and a different efficacy endpoint (severe disease, not viral load), and the study's authors say immunomodulators, possibly with antivirals, are heading to Phase 3 for preventing severe dengue. Separately, Florida recorded 485 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, up from 62 the year before. Key Elements Leah KatzelnikVincent RacanielloAndrew MehleScience Translational MedicineCell ReportsDengvaxiaSanofiRIG-Iantibody-dependent enhancementenvelope dimer epitope (EDE)Aedes aegyptiCIDRAP314 Action FundAmy ActonAbdul El-Sayed A dengue study that overturns what vaccine developers were optimizing for Dengue has defeated more vaccine programs than almost any pathogen in modern virology, and a new controlled human infection study published in Science Translational Medicine suggests the industry may have been measuring the wrong thing. In 45 healthy adults challenged with an attenuated dengue-3 strain, the people who mounted the weakest long-term immunity were the ones whose virus replicated the most — and the best, most durable responses came from those in the middle, not the top, of the viremia range. "The rapid activation of the adaptive effector functions come at the expense of developing high-quality enduring adaptive immunity," said Vincent Racaniello, a Columbia University virologist, describing the paper's central finding on This Week in Virology. That sentence inverts a decade of vaccine intuition. If high viral replication produces a fast, strong immune blitz that then collapses, then designing a dengue vaccine to maximize replication — or to maximize raw antibody titer — is not just suboptimal. It may be actively counterproductive. The mechanism runs through IL-12 and a B-cell shortcut The study, whose senior author is Leah Katzelnik, measured 80 distinct immune parameters and sorted participants into three groups based on how much virus they produced. The pattern that emerged was stark. Viremia group n Dominant prior immunity Antibody / T-cell outcome Low (near zero) 8 Mostly polytypic (multiple prior infections) Potent neutralizing antibodies against conserved quaternary epitopes; minimal replication Intermediate 12 Mostly heterotypic Greatest expansion of dengue-specific CD8 cells; most persistent neutralizing antibodies High 11 Mostly heterotypic Highest plasmablast expansion, fastest antibody decay, T-cell collapse by day 28–90 The high-viremia group drove elevated IL-12/IL-23 at day 9 — a signal that pushed B cells down a shortcut toward short-lived plasmablasts rather than the high-affinity, long-lived plasma cells that actually protect you years later. The same pathway had been described before in Salmonella infection. By day 28 and day 90, activated interferon-gamma-positive T cells had collapsed in that group. The intermediate group, by contrast, peaked at day 28: slower, but built to last. For vaccine developers, the practical instruction is unambiguous. "As you're developing that vaccine, you shouldn't necessarily optimize replication level or antibody level, because you need to have this balance between a few different types of responses to get the best long-term memory response," said Brienne Barker of Drew University. Antibody-dependent enhancement is the master switch — and a cheap lab test can find it Dengue's four serotypes are what make it so treacherous. Antibodies from a first infection can bind a second serotype without neutralizing it, acting as a Trojan horse that ferries the virus into Fc-receptor-bearing immune cells it otherwise couldn't infect. The result is higher viral load and, in severe cases, plasma leak, shock, hemorrhage and death. Racaniello noted this dynamic has wrecked multiple prior dengue vaccine programs. "Antibody-dependent enhancement inhibits intracellular antiviral responses and produces a barren immune signaling, enabling the virus to replicate more without triggering a normal, innate, and adaptive response," he said. The trial found that the single strongest linear predictor of viremia was fold enhancement of dengue-3 infection by participant serum at a 1:10 dilution, measured in cells engineered to express all three Fc receptors. Neutralizing antibody titers to dengue-3, meanwhile, predicted protection. Crucially, even mild enhancement mattered. "Any amount of antibody-dependent enhancement, even mild, hampers the antiviral responses," Racaniello said. "And that's associated with delayed and sustained inflammation that can get worse and worse." That is why the assay result carries commercial weight far beyond this one trial. Because the cell-culture readout lined up with what actually happened in human volunteers, developers may be able to screen vaccine candidates for enhancement risk before ever running a human study. "This paper also validates a set of tools for assaying your vaccine candidates in easier ways than doing the challenge studies, which you would presumably then do to test safety of the vaccine," said Alan Dove, one of the show's hosts. The authors go further: they write that early therapeutic immunomodulation, possibly combined with antivirals, could limit replication and improve long-term immunity, and that such drugs will soon be evaluated in Phase 3 trials to prevent progression to severe dengue. Barker's caveat is the one that will define those trials — any immune damper must not suppress the responses needed for durable memory. The broadly protective antibody only appears after repeat infection The study's second uncomfortable finding concerns the envelope dimer epitope, or EDE — a quaternary site spanning two envelope proteins that is conserved across all four serotypes and broadly neutralizing. Only participants with more than one prior dengue infection carried EDE antibodies, and those who had them showed minimal replication after challenge. The implication for vaccine design is a hard constraint: a dengue vaccine must induce responses to all four serotypes, because it is sequential exposure that generates the broadly active antibodies. A two-serotype or partially cross-reactive vaccine will not get there. Antibodies to the non-structural protein NS1 told a parallel story. Participants with NS1 binding breadth — typically people who had lived in endemic areas — partially controlled replication. The authors argue that vaccines inducing humoral and possibly cellular immunity to non-structural proteins like NS1 may not reduce viremia at all, yet could still prevent severe disease. That reframes the endpoint problem. If an NS1-based vaccine doesn't lower viral load but stops people from ending up in the hospital, then viral load is the wrong yardstick for judging it. The same logic applies to the study's broader takeaway: what matters is whether the immune response left behind is durable, not whether it was loud. A trial that the word "challenge" makes sound scarier than it was The 45 participants at the NIH in Bethesda received 103 ± 10^0.5 PFU of an attenuated dengue-3 vaccine candidate — rDEN3-Δ30-31-7164, which carries a 30-base deletion in the 3' non-coding region — by subcutaneous injection in the deltoid. Samples were drawn at days 0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 28, 57, 90, 180 and 365. Three naive participants received a lower dose. One participant developed a Staphylococcus aureus foot infection at day 328, unrelated to the challenge. The construct is called "full-length" because, unlike Sanofi's Dengvaxia — which uses a yellow fever backbone and carries only dengue structural proteins — all dengue proteins are present. Racaniello objected that the paper never explains this point for non-specialists. The hosts also pushed back on the framing itself. Barker and Dove both reacted with alarm to the phrase "dengue challenge study" before realizing every participant got an attenuated vaccine strain, not wild-type virus. Barker called it "click-bait-y." Dove put it more bluntly: "you challenged with a vaccine — no, that's a vaccine trial." The paper references 11 prior dengue challenge studies, all using attenuated viruses, because wild-type dengue cannot ethically be given to volunteers. Dove conceded the term is defensible, since giving even an attenuated strain to someone with prior dengue carries real enhancement risk — the trial's primary safety question. Influenza's nucleoprotein is hiding the cell's own alarm signals The episode's second paper, in Cell Reports from Andrew Mehle's lab at the University of Wisconsin–Madison (with Institut Pasteur and Dalhousie University), describes a countermeasure that works against the host's own RNA rather than the virus's. RIG-I is the immune sensor that patrols the cytoplasm for double-stranded RNA bearing a 5' di- or triphosphate. Because cellular RNA vastly outnumbers RIG-I molecules, the sensor cycles rapidly on and off harmless RNA and commits only when it finds that phosphate mark. Using a quantitative crosslinking-immunoprecipitation-sequencing method, first authors Mitchell Ledwith and Thomas Nipper found that even in infected cells, most RIG-I-bound RNAs are host-derived — mainly small non-coding RNAs made by RNA polymerase III, including Y RNAs, VTRNAs, U6, Alu and tRNAs. Infection increases the share of these small RNAs that keep a 5' triphosphate, making them immunogenic and amplifying the interferon response. Influenza nucleoprotein binds those same RNAs. NP and RIG-I co-immunoprecipitate, and the interaction requires RNA. About 25% of NP-bound reads in infected cells are host-derived, and comparing NP expressed alone with NP in infected cells turned up 1,400 differentially bound RNAs — showing infection reshapes NP's RNA partners. Functionally, RNAs pulled down with NP from infected cells activate an interferon promoter reporter; the same RNAs from uninfected cells do not. Treating the RNA with RNase or stripping the 5' triphosphate abolishes activation. A cytoplasm-restricted NP construct completely blocks sensing of triphosphate double-stranded RNA. The authors replicated the findings in primary human bronchial epithelial cells grown at air-liquid interface, though not in animals. Dove's analogy is that the Pol III transcripts act like a transistor's bias voltage, setting RIG-I's sensitivity so that a viral signal pushes it over threshold. Spindler frames it as the system training on itself. The authors note that all negative-strand RNA viruses carry an NP or N protein, and that some positive-strand viruses such as coronaviruses bind RNA without sequence specificity — suggesting a shared strategy worth testing. Florida's 485 local dengue cases are the number to watch CIDRAP reported 485 autochthonous dengue cases in Florida in 2026, up from 62 the prior year. Racaniello attributes the rise to Aedes aegypti range expansion and a base of infected people large enough to sustain transmission, and he expects spread further north. Barker noted there were zero autochthonous cases when she began teaching at Drew. Dove stressed this is not a vaccine-uptake failure: no highly efficacious dengue vaccine exists. Separately, six doctors and public health professionals won seats in the 2026 US midterms with support from the 314 Action Fund, including Amy Acton as Ohio governor, Abdul El-Sayed as a Michigan senator, pediatrician Ann Andrews for South Carolina Senate, Richard Pan in California, nurse Mitchell Berman in Wisconsin, nurse practitioner Christina Knickerbocker in Ohio, surgeon Adam Hamawy in New Jersey's 12th District, and microbiologist Jasmine Clark in the Georgia House. Dove cautioned that physicians in Congress are a mixed bag. Listener mail covered a pro-vaccine mother in Florida who asked why nobody in her Facebook moms group mentions the RSV vaccine when mothers describe infants hospitalized with RSV; the hosts' consensus was that raising vaccination mid-crisis is poorly timed, but a follow-up note that a vaccine exists for children from six months could prevent the next hospitalization. Racaniello added that natural RSV infection does not confer good immunity. A third-year biomedicine student in Australia credited the show with cementing his interest in virology research and called Operation Warp Speed the greatest public health achievement in his memory. Another listener sent David Morens' article on measles in Fiji in 1875, which recorded roughly 50,000 deaths in a population of 150,000 — about a third — after the islands were annexed to the British Empire; Dove noted Jack London's South Sea Tales contains accounts of measles deliberately introduced to island populations. What to watch next Three threads carry forward. First, the Phase 3 trials of immunomodulators to prevent severe dengue, which the paper says are imminent — their design will test whether the IL-12/plasmablast pathway is a viable target or whether blunting it costs durable immunity. Second, whether the Fc-receptor enhancement assay becomes a standard gate for dengue vaccine candidates, given that it predicted human viremia from a cell-culture readout. Third, whether NP's blockade of host self-RNA sensing generalizes, which would make it a broad antiviral-target class rather than an influenza curiosity. On the public-health side, Florida's jump from 62 to 485 cases in a single year is the figure that matters for anyone tracking US vector-borne disease exposure — and for the vaccine developers whose market is quietly moving north. Leer en español “As of Oct. 30, 904 cases (of dengue), of which 60% have been acquired in the state of Florida, and that’s quite unusual,” said Florida International University Infectious Disease Expert Dr. Aileen Marty. “So this is dramatically more than last year, although last year was a banner year as well.” When it comes to dengue cases currently being tracked across the country, Florida is a national leader. “We actually have had all four dengue virus types in Florida,” said Marty. “Just overwhelmingly type two and overwhelmingly this particular subtype that’s very dangerous.” Marty went on to explain that the majority of cases are now being acquired in Florida, as opposed to international travel-associated cases. “So in Florida, from this particular outbreak this year, one individual died in Hillsborough County, an elderly woman,” she said. An increase in dengue cases acquired in Florida has been primarily driven by an outbreak in the Tampa area, with 407 cases out of Hillsborough County. Cases in South Florida are comparatively lower, with Miami-Dade County at 12 cases and Broward County with just one reported case. “It is good, and Broward, for example, is phenomenal,” said Marty. “We have drones that can deliver targeted bacillus thuringiensis to kill off larvae in people’s little lagoons or what have you, or plant areas, and also spray anti-mosquito products targeted to exactly the mosquitoes.” Marty added that the rising global temperatures are raising the stakes. “It has to do with the hotter temperatures, which facilitates the growth of mosquitoes, such that you get new generations of mosquitoes in much shorter periods of time and they’re thirstier, so they bite more,” she said. “Because when it’s hot, the mosquitoes, like all animals, get thirsty.” More from Dr. Marty Other reasons for more cases: “It’s a reflection of where there were mosquitoes that were resistant to permethrin, which is a problem now in Florida, which is one of the anti-mosquito products that we use. So that’s a problem. It’s not a mosquito repellent you would put on your skin ever, but it is a very valuable, otherwise mosquito product that these mosquitoes are resistant to so some of the spraying doesn’t work.” On Hillsborough spike: “Demand governmental action so that, for example, there’s something called bacillus thuringiensis, which is a bacterium. You can buy it on Amazon, Home Depot, Lowe’s, what have you. And these little, you buy them as little packets, you throw it in water that you can’t remove in your area, and it kills the larva of the mosquitoes in your area. That helps reduce the problem for you. And let me add that that is another reason that we saw so many in that particular region of Hillsborough County. And that is, it’s a poor area where people often don’t have the wherewithal themselves to spray their areas and may not have the time or ability to get rid of water sources where the mosquitoes are laying their eggs.” How to prevent infection: Marty said it could take between three days and two weeks to see the symptoms. Things to do around your home include making sure there is no standing water. You can also place a drop of olive oil in plants where standing water can gather, like orchids, and she said not to drink beer outside as that can attract mosquitos. Marty said there are some groups at higher risk to dengue, including those who are immune compromised, but also pregnant women. She said if you are pregnant and showing signs of dengue fever to see a doctor or go to hospital immediately. Tel: 024 3772 7988 Fax: (024) 37722734 Email: evnn@vietnamnet.vn Talkshow Hồ sơ Ảnh Video Multimedia Podcast Tuyến bài Sự kiện nóng Tuyển dụng Liên hệ tòa soạn Liên hệ quảng cáo Đăng nhập x Aa Facebook Zalo Email Copy Link Aa Aa Vietnamnet global 07/11/2026 08:39 (GMT+07:00) Vietnam reports over 170,000 dengue cases as outbreaks defy seasonal patterns Copy link 07/11/2026 08:39 (GMT+07:00) Vietnam has recorded more than 170,000 dengue cases and 21 deaths in the first 10 months of 2026, with experts warning that outbreaks are becoming increasingly unpredictable and no longer follow traditional seasonal patterns. Dengue outbreaks becoming increasingly unpredictable Vietnam's dengue situation is growing more complicated, with infections spreading widely and no longer following their usual seasonal cycles. In 2025, the country recorded the highest number of dengue cases in the Asia-Pacific region. On November 6, the Ministry of Health's Department of Disease Prevention, in coordination with relevant organizations, held the Dengue Summit 2026 to assess the disease burden and discuss prevention strategies. According to reports presented at the event, dengue is among the world's fastest-growing mosquito-borne infectious diseases, with an estimated 100 million to 400 million infections annually. In Vietnam, dengue has remained a persistent public health challenge for more than four decades. Since 1980, the country has recorded hundreds of thousands of cases, with deaths reported every year. The incidence of dengue per 100,000 people is considerably higher than that of many other infectious diseases. It ranks first in incidence and second in mortality among infectious diseases in Vietnam. Speaking at the conference, Hoang Minh Duc, Director of the Ministry of Health's Department of Disease Prevention, said the country had recorded more than 170,000 dengue infections and 21 deaths since the beginning of 2026. Despite years of resource mobilization, extensive technical interventions and support from domestic and international experts, dengue outbreaks have not been controlled as effectively as expected. Professor Nguyen Van Kinh, President of the Vietnam Society of Infectious Diseases, said infections had continued to rise significantly following the major outbreak in 2022. More concerning, the current increase in dengue cases no longer follows the seasonal or cyclical patterns observed in previous years. Kinh identified climate change and increased rainfall as major contributing factors. Mosquito species responsible for transmitting dengue, particularly Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, readily lay eggs in stagnant water, including rainwater collected in containers and other locations. Increased rainfall therefore creates favorable breeding conditions, allowing mosquito populations to expand and raising the risk of outbreaks. High disease burden complicates dengue prevention efforts Although Vietnam has reported more than 170,000 dengue cases this year, the number of deaths remains relatively low, with a reported fatality rate of approximately 0.01%. Nevertheless, experts warn that the disease's clinical progression remains complex and difficult to predict. Compared with other infectious diseases, dengue represents a substantial public health burden in Vietnam and could continue to pose challenges for many years, Kinh said. One major difficulty, according to the professor, is that more than 90% of infected individuals show no clinical symptoms. As a result, people who are unaware of their infection may still contribute to transmission when mosquitoes bite them and subsequently spread the virus to others. Kinh also stressed that completely eliminating mosquitoes and their larvae is virtually impossible, regardless of the intensity of control efforts. "As long as the source of infection and the vectors transmitting the disease remain, dengue will continue to exist," he said. He believes vaccines offer significant potential as an additional preventive measure to help bring outbreaks under better control. To address the challenge, Kinh recommended that Vietnam's healthcare sector coordinate three major strategies: dengue vaccination, mosquito and larval control to reduce infections, and timely, effective treatment to minimize deaths. He emphasized the importance of eliminating mosquito breeding sites while ensuring patients receive medical attention without delay. "Without mosquito larvae, there is no dengue transmission. And treatment for dengue patients must never be delayed," Kinh stressed. N. supplementary_news.content: Severe liver damage due to dengue fever. Two female patients, aged 23 and 53, were transferred to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases with severe dengue fever. Both had severely low platelet counts, elevated liver enzymes of nearly 2,000 U/L, along with coagulation disorders and signs of organ damage. Notably, the disease can worsen even when the patient's fever begins to subside. Báo Pháp Luật Việt Nam • 11/11/2026 Patient BH (53 years old, Hai Phong ) was previously healthy and had never had dengue fever. Approximately 5 days before hospitalization, she experienced a persistent high fever, sometimes reaching 39–40°C, accompanied by general body aches, nausea, frequent vomiting, and abdominal pain. The patient self-medicated with paracetamol at home, but their condition did not improve. Upon arriving at a medical facility, tests confirmed a Dengue virus infection, and a rapid decrease in platelet count from 38 to 21 G/L was observed. Liver enzymes were also elevated. Due to the complicated situation, the patient was transferred to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases. At the hospital, the patient still had a high fever, severe pain in the right lower rib area, and petechiae (small hemorrhagic spots) appeared under the skin at the injection site. Tests showed platelet count was only 23 G/L, AST was elevated to 1,939 U/L, ALT was 804 U/L, along with coagulation disorders. Patients diagnosed with severe dengue hemorrhagic fever, liver damage, and coagulation disorders require close monitoring for the risk of bleeding, circulatory disturbances, and other complications. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA Another case involves a 23-year-old female patient, PL, from Hanoi , who was previously healthy. Approximately 7 days before being transferred to the hospital, the patient developed intermittent high fever, sometimes reaching 39°C, accompanied by chills, headache, body aches, abdominal pain, nausea, frequent vomiting, and loose stools. Following previous treatment at a medical facility, the patient's condition did not improve, and laboratory test results continued to deteriorate. Platelets decreased to 21 G/L; AST increased to 1,907 U/L and ALT to 883 U/L. Notably, the ultrasound results revealed fluid in the abdominal cavity and bilateral pleural spaces. This could be indicative of plasma leakage – a crucial mechanism in severe dengue hemorrhagic fever, which can lead to decreased circulating volume, hemodynamic instability, and shock if not detected and treated promptly. Upon transfer to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, the patient still had a fever, was very tired, had petechiae (small hemorrhagic spots) under the skin, and experienced pain in the liver area. Doctors assessed this as a severe case of Dengue hemorrhagic fever with serious liver damage, requiring close monitoring and intensive treatment. You may also like Warning: Severe thrombocytopenia and serious liver damage due to dengue fever. Among the 16 dengue fever patients currently being treated at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, many cases have developed severe symptoms, including liver damage requiring intensive treatment. Dengue fever can worsen; be vigilant during the fever-reducing phase. Many dengue fever patients require emergency treatment with severely low platelet counts, liver damage, and blood clotting disorders, even though they were previously perfectly healthy. 23-year-old girl in critical condition with dengue fever, doctors warn. (Dan Tri Newspaper) - After high fevers, two previously healthy women were hospitalized with severe Dengue hemorrhagic fever, severely low platelet count, blood clotting disorders, and serious liver damage. Just because the fever has subsided doesn't mean the illness is out of danger. Currently, the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases is treating 16 patients with dengue fever, including some severe cases requiring close monitoring and intensive treatment. According to Dr. Pham Van Phuc, Deputy Director of the Intensive Care Unit at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, dengue fever is an infectious disease caused by the dengue virus, primarily transmitted through Aedes mosquitoes. The disease can occur at all ages, including those who were previously completely healthy. According to Dr. Phuc, thrombocytopenia (low platelet count) is a common symptom in dengue fever patients, but the severity of the disease cannot be assessed solely based on platelet count. The risk of complications needs to be evaluated holistically based on clinical condition and many other indicators such as signs of bleeding, blood pressure, pulse, urine output, blood concentration, and signs of organ damage. "In these two cases, in addition to a sharp drop in platelets, the patients also had very high liver enzymes, blood clotting disorders, and other warning signs. These abnormalities indicate that the disease has progressed seriously and requires close monitoring to detect and treat complications promptly," Dr. Phuc said. In particular, one of the key points to note about dengue fever is that the disease can worsen when the patient's fever begins to subside. The dangerous phase usually occurs between the 3rd and 7th day of the illness, when the patient may experience plasma leakage, severe bleeding, or organ damage. If not detected and treated promptly, severe plasma leakage can lead to hypovolemia, shock, multiple organ failure, and be life-threatening. Dr. Phuc emphasized that patients and their families should not assess the severity of the illness based solely on body temperature. A reduction in fever does not necessarily mean the illness has passed the critical stage. People who have or suspect they have dengue fever should go to a medical facility immediately if they experience warning signs such as severe or persistent abdominal pain, frequent vomiting, lethargy or restlessness, nosebleeds, bleeding gums, decreased urination, cold hands and feet, or extreme fatigue. You may also like If a doctor instructs the patient to monitor and treat the condition at home, the patient should rest, stay adequately hydrated, monitor their temperature, appetite, urine output, and any unusual symptoms. Do not increase the dosage of fever-reducing medication or use anti-inflammatory drugs without a doctor's prescription, as some medications can increase the risk of bleeding in dengue fever. Attending scheduled follow-up appointments, undergoing prescribed tests, and closely monitoring the patient during the 3rd to 7th day are crucial for early detection of the risk of worsening condition. Patients should not be complacent when their fever subsides or symptoms seem to improve, as this could be the time when the disease enters a dangerous stage. To proactively prevent dengue fever, people need to implement several measures simultaneously, such as eliminating stagnant water sources, destroying mosquito larvae, limiting mosquito bites, and maintaining a clean living environment. In addition, dengue vaccination is a proactive preventive measure that people can choose according to the instructions of healthcare workers and the regulations of vaccination centers. However, vaccination does not replace mosquito control measures and prevention of mosquito bites. If dengue fever symptoms are suspected, people should still go to a medical facility for examination, testing, and appropriate monitoring guidance. Dengue fever can be severe at any age. Early recognition of warning signs, especially between the 3rd and 7th day, following proper monitoring guidelines, and seeking timely medical attention are crucial factors in limiting complications and protecting the health and lives of patients. Proactive prevention, combining mosquito control measures with appropriate vaccination, will contribute to reducing the risk of contracting and experiencing severe dengue fever. The incidence rate per 100,000 people is significantly higher than other infectious diseases, ranking first in incidence and second in mortality among infectious diseases in Vietnam. Check Symptoms Speaking at the conference, Dr. Hoang Minh Duc, Director of the Department of Disease Prevention (Ministry of Health), said that since the beginning of the year, the whole country has exceeded 170,000 cases of infection along with 21 deaths. He stated that, despite years of focusing on mobilizing resources, implementing a series of technical measures, and receiving active support from domestic and international experts, the epidemic has not yet been controlled as effectively as desired. You may also like Further analyzing this situation, Professor Nguyen Van Kinh, President of the Vietnam Infectious Diseases Association, said that after the outbreak in 2022, the number of cases continued to increase significantly. Check Symptoms Notably, the current trend of increasing cases no longer follows a seasonal or cyclical pattern as it did in the past. According to Mr. Kinh, one of the core causes identified is climate change leading to increased rainfall. Mosquito species such as Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus prefer to lay their eggs in stagnant water, especially rainwater, creating a favorable environment for mosquitoes to breed, thrive, and cause outbreaks. The burden of disease and the challenge of prevention and control. The number of cases recorded this year has exceeded 170,000, while the death rate remains low at approximately 0.01%. However, according to experts, clinical reality shows that the disease's progression remains complex and unpredictable. Find Treatments When compared to other infectious diseases, Professor Kinh believes that dengue fever is a major disease burden in Vietnam and may continue to be so for many years to come. A major reason is that "over 90% of patients are asymptomatic." Therefore, they unwittingly become a source of infection when bitten by mosquitoes and continue to transmit the virus to others. You may also like Spraying insecticide to kill mosquitoes in Hanoi . Photo: N.Huyen "Furthermore, despite all efforts, completely eradicating mosquitoes and larvae is almost impossible. As long as the source and vectors of the disease remain, the epidemic will continue to exist. Therefore, the greatest hope now rests on vaccines as a powerful preventive tool to gradually control the epidemic more effectively," Professor Kinh emphasized. To address this challenge, experts recommend that the health sector closely coordinate three key solutions: firstly, vaccination; secondly, mosquito and larva eradication to reduce the number of cases; and thirdly, timely and effective treatment to minimize mortality rates. "Without mosquito larvae, there is no dengue fever, and we must not delay treatment for dengue fever patients," Professor Kinh emphasized. In the first 10 months of 2026, the whole country recorded more than 170,000 cases of dengue fever and 21 deaths. Đặt vắc xin Người Đưa Tin•06/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 On November 6th, the Department of Disease Prevention ( Ministry of Health ) co-organized the Dengue Summit 2026 with the theme "Dengue in Action: Applying Science to Practice Towards Comprehensive Dengue Management". Over 170,000 cases of dengue fever and 21 deaths. Dengue fever is one of the fastest-growing infectious diseases transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes worldwide , with approximately 100-400 million cases annually. In Vietnam, dengue fever has been a persistent burden for over four decades. Since 1980, the country has recorded hundreds of thousands of cases annually, with deaths occurring every year. The incidence rate of dengue fever per 100,000 population is much higher than that of other infectious diseases – ranking first in incidence and second in mortality among infectious diseases in Vietnam. In 2025, Vietnam recorded 184,903 cases of dengue fever. The disease is endemic year-round in all provinces and cities, spreading to even the northern mountainous provinces such as Tuyen Quang and Son La - areas that previously recorded few cases. Tìm hiểu lịch sử Khám phá thêm Đặt vắc xin Tra cứu bệnh Chăm sóc sức khỏe Mr. Hoang Minh Duc - Director of the Department of Disease Prevention (Ministry of Health ) (Photo: Nguyen Thi). All four serotypes of the Dengue virus (DENV-1, 2, 3, 4) circulate in Vietnam, with the dominant serotype changing over time and across regions. The rotation of these serotypes, combined with climate change, rapid urbanization, and insecticide-resistant mosquitoes, makes Dengue fever increasingly difficult to predict. According to Dr. Hoang Minh Duc, Director of the Department of Disease Prevention (Ministry of Health), in the first 10 months of the year, the country recorded more than 170,000 cases of dengue fever and 21 deaths. This continues to be an endemic disease, and every year the health sector has to implement surveillance, prevention, and outbreak control activities in many localities. Chăm sóc sức khỏe The conference scene (Photo: Nguyen Thi). Mr. Duc also expressed his concern that, after many years of mobilizing resources, implementing technical measures, and receiving support from domestic and international experts, dengue fever has still not been controlled as effectively as desired. Đặt vắc xin You may also like For a long time, disease prevention efforts focused primarily on measures to eliminate mosquitoes, kill mosquito larvae and pupae, and monitor epidemiological indicators. According to the Director, these measures need to be maintained while simultaneously updating with new contingency plans. Referring to the dengue fever vaccine, he said that this is a measure that the health sector is very interested in. In the field of disease prevention, vaccination is one of the most important preventive measures. Dengue fever remains a significant disease burden. Professor Nguyen Van Kinh, former Director of the Central Hospital for Tropical Diseases, believes that dengue fever remains a significant disease burden in Vietnam and may continue for many years to come. According to this expert, after the outbreak in 2022, the number of cases continued to increase significantly. Notably, the disease trend no longer follows a clear seasonal or cyclical pattern as before. Tra cứu bệnh Professor Kính informed the conference that dengue fever is unpredictable and still causes deaths annually (Photo: Hoàng Bích). One of the factors mentioned is climate change, which alters rainfall patterns and creates more favorable conditions for disease-carrying mosquitoes to breed. Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes typically lay their eggs in stagnant water, including rainwater-collecting containers. Mr. Kinh stated that the clinical course of dengue fever is very complex, depending on the immune response, age, and underlying medical conditions of each individual. Another difficulty is that many people infected with the Dengue virus do not show clinical symptoms. According to Professor Kinh, more than 90% of infected people may not exhibit symptoms, but they can still become a source of infection when bitten by mosquitoes, which then transmit the virus to others. Meanwhile, completely eliminating mosquitoes and larvae is difficult to achieve. As long as the source of the disease and the vectors remain, the risk of the disease continuing to persist remains. Currently, there is no specific treatment for dengue fever. Treatment mainly focuses on controlling symptoms, closely monitoring the patient's condition, and promptly managing complications, especially shock. The important goal is to prevent the patient from progressing to a severe stage, to overcome shock, and to promote recovery. You may also like Therefore, vaccines are expected to become a more effective tool in supporting disease control. Professor Dr. Nguyen Van Kinh - former Director of the Central Hospital for Tropical Diseases (Photo: Hoang Bich). Combining proactive preventive measures simultaneously is seen as a policy signal consistent with WHO recommendations on an integrated dengue control strategy. Mr. Benjamin Ping, General Director of Takeda Vietnam, shared that although awareness of dengue fever in Vietnam is relatively high, research shows that the majority of people still do not fully understand the risks and severity of the disease for themselves and their families, as well as the urgency of proactive prevention. "Therefore, it is necessary to strengthen proactive preventive measures to reduce the burden of dengue fever in Vietnam. Takeda is collaborating with international partners and health agencies to support evidence- based prevention solutions aimed at protecting public health, with vaccination being part of the overall disease prevention and control strategy," said Benjamin Ping. Given that dengue fever occurs year-round, experts are calling for the synchronized implementation of proactive prevention measures at all levels, from strengthening epidemiological surveillance and improving treatment capacity to communicating behavioral changes and encouraging appropriate vaccination. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 12, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Study Identifies Twenty-Eight Sub-Municipal Dengue Clusters Across Colombia’s Valle del Cauca by November 11, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Study Identifies Twenty-Eight Sub-Municipal Dengue Clusters Across Colombia's Valle del Cauca Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Researchers examining the transmission of dengue virus in Colombia’s department of Valle del Cauca identified twenty-eight localized disease clusters occurring at the sub-municipal level throughout 2022. The retrospective observational study evaluated laboratory-confirmed cases to map the precise geographic and temporal dimensions of infection, providing critical spatial resolution for public health agencies aiming to deploy reactive vector control measures. By analyzing geographic coordinates linked to patient residences alongside official consultation dates, the investigative team demonstrated that local transmission events routinely concentrate within tightly defined neighborhood boundaries while persisting across shifting climatic periods. Dengue remains an endemic public health concern throughout Valle del Cauca, yet the exact spatial scale and temporal timing of seasonal transmission necessary to execute effective reactive interventions have historically remained unclear across the department’s forty-two municipalities. To resolve this operational gap, the authors established two primary research aims. The first focused on identifying statistically significant spatio-temporal dengue clusters within defined municipal zones. The secondary aim evaluated the relationship between patients’ demographic and clinical characteristics and their likelihood of requiring hospitalization for dengue care. The investigation drew data directly from the Sistema Nacional de Vigilancia en Salud Pública, Colombia’s national public health surveillance network known as SIVIGILA. Healthcare providers across Valle del Cauca reported a total of 3,964 dengue cases during the 2022 calendar year, of which 2,232 cases—or 56 percent—were confirmed through laboratory diagnostics. For the purpose of spatial analysis, the investigators utilized each patient’s documented residential geolocation as the probable site of viral infection. Among the laboratory-confirmed records, 1,973 cases fell within the specified spatial boundaries of nine municipalities selected for detailed clustering assessment, which was executed using Kulldorff’s space-time scan statistic and mapped using the R programming environment. The space-time scan statistic uncovered twenty-eight distinct clusters at the sub-municipal level, encompassing radii between 0 and 0.98 kilometers. These transmission foci endured for durations spanning one to six months and contained case counts ranging from 10 to 114 individuals. In total, the identified clusters accounted for 32.0 percent of the 1,973 cases analyzed within the nine municipalities. Notably, twenty-six of the twenty-eight clusters—representing 92.9 percent—spanned both warm-dry and cool-wet seasonal phases, demonstrating that localized viral activity regularly bridged contrasting meteorological periods rather than confining itself exclusively to a single seasonal window. Beyond mapping spatial boundaries, the research team analyzed factors driving severe disease manifestations, noting that 960 patients within the overall cohort were hospitalized. Multivariable evaluations revealed substantial disparities across socioeconomic brackets and age groups. Patients classified within a lower socioeconomic status faced an estimated 30 percent increase in the odds of hospitalization compared to individuals of higher economic standing, with an odds ratio of 1.30 and a 95 percent confidence interval between 1.07 and 1.57. Furthermore, individuals enrolled in Colombia’s state-subsidized health insurance scheme exhibited significantly elevated odds of hospital admission compared to those participating in the contributory insurance system, reflected by an odds ratio of 1.74 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.41 to 2.15. Age also represented a key determinant of clinical escalation, as individuals aged 70 years or older experienced more than double the odds of hospital admission compared to younger adults between the ages of 20 and 29 years, yielding an odds ratio of 2.47 and a 95 percent confidence interval from 1.51 to 4.04. The authors concluded that pinpointing sub-municipal dengue clusters reveals highly actionable spatial targets capable of guiding reactive local mosquito control programs, while underscoring that dengue places an unequal burden on socioeconomically vulnerable communities and older populations in Valle del Cauca. supplementary_news.content: Skip to content Main Navigation Search Search for: Local Weather Video On Your Side Investigates Responds Newsletters TV Listings Watch 24/7 Create profile / Log in Dashboard Email preferences Sign out Trending Elections Property Taxes Affordability YouTube Hurricane Season Newsletters 📺Watch News 24/7 🔎 Send a Tip Expand Florida More than 500 people have gotten dengue in Florida this year. How does infection spread? By Madison Czopek | Politifact • Published November 9, 2026 • Updated on November 9, 2026 at 1:40 pm BOOKMARKER The NBC6 South Florida News streaming channel plays local South Florida news 24 hours a day, seven days a week. On Nov. 5, low flying helicopters blanketed areas of Florida’s Pinellas and Hillsborough counties, Florida, with a fine mist. It’s one of the ways Florida health officials hope to slow the country’s largest dengue fever outbreak in more than a decade. Dengue starts with a mosquito bite, so killing the insects is key. The helicopters spray water mixed with Bti, a natural bacteria found in soil that kills black fly and mosquito larvae. Watch NBC6 free wherever you are WATCH HERE Most people become infected when traveling in high dengue risk areas, and Florida had recorded 382 international travel-associated cases as of Oct. 31. But the state has also counted a recent record high number of people infected on Florida’s turf: 524. Florida has had domestic dengue outbreaks before. In 2010, it counted 58 locally acquired cases, after nearly eight decades of reprieve. Since then, the largest outbreak was in 2023, when the state reported 189 dengue cases contracted in Florida. As Florida navigates its largest dengue outbreak in more than 15 years, it might help to understand how this virus spreads and how to recognize symptoms and protect yourself. We sought answers to some pressing dengue fever questions. What is dengue fever? Dengue fever can develop after a person is infected with any of the four dengue viruses. The virus is not transmitted person-to-person, and there is no widely available vaccine to prevent infection. Local Broward County 42 minutes ago NBCUniversal Local Impact Grant helps Ranger Good Works help more kids in need Veterans Day 1 hour ago Veterans share 25-year breakfast tradition at Miami McDonald's About 3 in 4 people do not get sick, but if symptoms develop, they typically set in about four to 10 days after an infected mosquito’s bite. The most common symptoms of mild dengue fever include high fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, rash, pain behind the eyes and muscle, joint and bone pain. About 1 in 20 people infected with a dengue virus develops a more severe form of dengue fever sometimes called dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome. Severe dengue is a life-threatening medical emergency that can cause shock, internal bleeding and death. Warning signs of a severe infection include serious stomach pain or tenderness, vomiting at least three times in 24 hours, bleeding from the gums or nose, rapid breathing, blood in stool or vomit, restlessness, feeling extremely tired and bleeding under the skin that might appear as purplish spots or patches. Those symptoms typically happen 24 to 48 hours after the fever, and they often come on quickly. Anyone experiencing them should seek immediate medical care. What is the treatment for dengue fever? There is no specific cure or treatment. Most people recover in about one week, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said. The CDC recommends people rest, hydrate, and take acetaminophen to reduce fever and pain. Avoid other pain relievers such as aspirin and ibuprofen because they can raise the risk of bleeding. For severe dengue fever, medical professionals might monitor a patient’s blood pressure and platelet count and provide blood transfusions or intravenous fluid and electrolyte replacement. Can someone develop immunity to dengue? After being infected with a dengue virus, a person’s immune system learns to fight that type of virus, which helps protect them from reinfection with that same virus. But he or she could remain susceptible to the other three dengue viruses. A person might be asymptomatic or have mild symptoms during an initial dengue infection, and then develop more severe symptoms — or, in rare cases, dengue hemorrhagic fever — after being infected with a second type of dengue virus, said Kristi Miley, a University of Florida public health professor. “Dengue is a doozy, mainly because the second infection can be more dangerous than the first,” Katelyn Jetelina, an epidemiologist and public health expert, said in social media posts. Florida has documented all four dengue viruses since 2009. The type of dengue virus that’s predominantly circulating now “has been noted to cause more severe symptoms than the other three serotypes,” Miley said. Telemundo San Antonio Telemundo San Antonio Mosquito Control Operations Manager Chalmers Vasquez checks the water in a fountain outside a vacant house for mosquito larvae, July 15, 2010, in Miami Beach, Fla. At the time, Miami-Dade County health officials were reporting the first suspected local case of dengue fever in decades. (AP) Why are there so many cases in Florida this year? Florida’s climate and environment provides ideal conditions for the Aedes species mosquitoes that spread dengue to thrive. If someone travels to a dengue endemic country and becomes infected even asymptomatically, dengue can enter a community. When a mosquito bites a person infected with the dengue virus, it can introduce the virus to the local mosquito population. An infected female mosquito will remain infected for her life — and she can pass the virus to her eggs, which can result in more than 500 infected offspring, said Miley. “When you consider the multiplication equation here and add that to the amount of excessive rainfall that the state has been experiencing this late in the year, one can quickly see how an outbreak of this magnitude can happen,” she said. All told, the previous 16 years saw only 606 total locally acquired cases. “Studies are ongoing to better understand the factors contributing to the dengue activity being seen in Florida in 2026,” said Isabella White, a Florida Department of Health spokesperson. Does the risk extend beyond Florida? Yes. Not every state has the climate to support Aedes mosquito populations, but any state that does could potentially see local transmission of dengue. In 2025, CDC data showed locally acquired dengue in Florida, California and Arizona. In August, Virginia health officials reported a locally acquired dengue fever infection. Nassau County Police Department/Getty Images Nassau County Police Department/Getty Images (Information source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) How can people protect themselves and others against dengue? The mosquitoes that carry dengue breed in standing water, so health officials urge people to be vigilant about eliminating it around their homes. “Dump or cover any standing water — especially after each time it rains,” Miley said. Florida’s Department of Health recommends discarding old tires and drums, emptying and cleaning bird baths or pet water bowls at least once or twice a week and protecting vehicles and boats with tarps so water cannot accumulate. Prevent mosquito bites by using Environmental Protection Agency-registered insect repellants such as deet and picaridin and covering skin with shoes, socks, and long sleeves and pants. The mosquitoes known to carry dengue are often considered “day biters,” Miley said. If you suspect you’ve been infected with the dengue virus, seek medical attention and avoid exposure to mosquitoes for seven days following symptoms — that’s how long a person would be able to infect mosquitoes, enabling them to spread the disease, Miley said. The Tampa Bay area remains the epicenter of a nationwide Dengue Fever outbreak. Hundreds of cases have been reported in Hillsborough and Pinellas counties, but will an upcoming cold front help stop the spread? FOX 13's Blake DeVine reports. The Brief Cooler temperatures could temporarily slow mosquitoes spreading dengue across the Tampa Bay area, although experts say a freeze is needed to significantly reduce their population. Florida has recorded 524 locally acquired dengue cases this year, with Hillsborough County accounting for most infections. Hillsborough County has extended its local emergency through Nov. 12 as mosquito control crews continue aerial and ground treatments. TAMPA, Fla. - An incoming cold front could temporarily suppress the aggressive insects driving Florida's historic dengue fever outbreak, though health experts warn only freezing temperatures can stop transmission. Cold weather brings brief relief The backstory: The virus primarily spreads through infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which thrive in Florida's warm climate. Dr. Nicole Iovine, UF Health's chief epidemiologist, says the approaching cold front could help reduce mosquito activity without eliminating the insects. "The lower temperature helps because the mosquitoes will be less active," she said. "So, 50 degrees, that's good. But as far as actually killing off the population, you need at least one night of a good freeze." Travel sparks local transmission Dig deeper: Iovine says the outbreak is particularly unusual because locally acquired dengue cases have historically been concentrated in South Florida. She believes infected travelers may have introduced the virus to mosquitoes in the Tampa Bay area, allowing it to spread locally. Florida dengue numbers surge By the numbers: Florida has confirmed 524 locally acquired dengue cases this year, alongside more than 900 total illnesses when counting travel-related infections, according to the Florida Department of Health. Local case tallies include: Hillsborough County: 407 cases Pinellas County: 80 cases Pasco County: 4 cases Hillsborough steps up treatments What's next: Hillsborough County leads Florida in locally acquired infections and has extended its state of local emergency through Thursday, Nov. 12. Mosquito control crews are increasing aerial and ground treatments across the county, targeting both adult mosquitoes and larvae. Hillsborough County Mosquito Management senior environmental scientist Paolo Pecora says the county is working to interrupt the mosquito life cycle. "We want to knock down the adult mosquitoes that are actively spreading the virus," Pecora said. Pecora says targeted treatments have reduced Aedes aegypti mosquito populations by 97% in the East Lake area. Dengue symptoms Why you should care: Dengue symptoms can include severe headaches, body aches, fever, nausea, vomiting and a rash. Some infected people experience mild symptoms or none at all. Iovine says people experiencing these symptoms should contact a health care provider about testing, particularly if they have no respiratory symptoms. There is no specific antiviral medication to treat dengue. Doctors typically recommend rest, plenty of fluids and acetaminophen, commonly known as Tylenol, to help manage mild symptoms. Patients should avoid ibuprofen and aspirin because they can increase the risk of bleeding. Unusual bleeding, severe abdominal pain or persistent vomiting require immediate medical attention. Protecting homes from mosquitoes What you can do: Homeowners can protect their properties by dumping standing water from flowerpots, buckets, tires and outdoor bins. Anyone heading outdoors should wear long protective sleeves and apply bug repellent formulated with DEET or picaridin. Residents can check upcoming neighborhood spray routes on the Hillsborough County Mosquito Operations website. The Source: Information for this story came from data from the Florida Department of Health, statements from Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services, interviews with UF Health's chief epidemiologist and previous reporting on FOX 13.
